title: Data classes, equality, enums, objects
scopeHtml: Scope: data class generated members, copy/destructuring, == vs === and the equals/hashCode contract, enum classes (entries, when, EnumMap), object declarations, companion objects, data object (Kotlin 1.9+).

notes.title: What a data class generates
notes.html:
The idea. A data class is a class whose job is to hold values, so the compiler writes the boring code for you: comparing two objects by content, printing them readably, copying them and taking them apart.

data class User(val id: Long, val name: String, val email: String?)

From that one line the compiler generates:

  • equals(other) and hashCode(): content-based.
  • toString(): User(id=1, name=Asha, email=null).
  • componentN() functions (component1() = id, ...): they power destructuring.
  • copy(id = ..., name = ..., email = ...): a new object with some values changed, defaults taken from the current object.

Only the primary constructor counts. The generated members look at properties declared in the primary constructor and nothing else. A property in the class body does not take part in equals, hashCode, toString, copy or componentN.

data class Session(val userId: Long) {
    var lastSeen: Long = 0       // ignored by equals/hashCode/toString/copy
}

Rules. The primary constructor needs at least one parameter, every parameter must be val or var, and a data class cannot be abstract, open, sealed or inner. It may implement interfaces and extend a regular open class.

Decompiled hashCode and equals (shape).

public int hashCode() {
    int result = Long.hashCode(this.id);
    result = result * 31 + this.name.hashCode();
    result = result * 31 + (this.email == null ? 0 : this.email.hashCode());
    return result;
}
public boolean equals(Object o) {
    if (this == o) return true;
    if (!(o instanceof User)) return false;
    User u = (User) o;
    return id == u.id && Intrinsics.areEqual(name, u.name) && Intrinsics.areEqual(email, u.email);
}

Note the 31 * multiplier chain: field order matters for the hash, and the first thing equals does is the identity shortcut.

Where you see it. Retrofit/Moshi response models, Room @Entity classes, ViewModel UI state (data class FeedState(val items: List<Post>, val loading: Boolean)), Compose state holders. In Jetpack Compose, equal state lets the runtime skip recomposition because it compares with equals.

Real-life picture. A student ID card. Two cards with the same name, roll number and class describe the same student information, even though they are two pieces of plastic. A data class treats objects the way we treat ID cards: by what is written on them.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "all properties take part": only primary-constructor ones do.
  • Forgetting that toString does not show body properties, which makes logs misleading.
  • Claiming data classes are immutable: var properties are allowed; immutability is your choice.

notes.title: Structural versus referential equality
notes.html:
The idea. Kotlin has two meanings of "same":

  • a == b (structural): "do they have equal content?" It compiles to a?.equals(b) ?: (b === null), so it is null-safe.
  • a === b (referential): "are they literally the same object in memory?" It compiles to a reference comparison (if_acmp), no method call.
val a = User(1, "Asha", null)
val b = User(1, "Asha", null)
a == b     // true  (data class equals)
a === b    // false (two objects)

Details that matter.

  • == on a type that does not override equals falls back to Any.equals, which is identity: the same as ===. This is why plain classes compare "unequal" even with identical fields.
  • != is !(a == b); !== is the identity negation.
  • On Float/Double, == follows IEEE (NaN == NaN is false) when the static type is a primitive but uses equals (so NaN equals NaN, and 0.0 differs from -0.0) when the static type is Any or nullable/generic. A surprising edge for generic code.
  • For String, == compares characters; two equal strings built at runtime are usually not ===.

Where === is correct. Checking it is the same listener you registered (removeObserver), the same singleton, if (this === other) return true at the top of equals, and data object/enum comparisons (for enums == and === are equivalent, the compiler even optimises).

Industry usage. Compose's remember(key) and derivedStateOf rely on equals; DiffUtil.areContentsTheSame is usually old == new; StateFlow only emits when the new value is != the old one (it "conflates equal values"), which is why mutating a list in place and re-emitting the same instance never updates the UI.

Real-life picture. Identical twins: same description (== is true), different persons (=== is false).

Common interview traps.

  • Believing == in Kotlin is Java's ==: it is equals.
  • Using === on strings or boxed numbers.
  • StateFlow.value = sameListInstanceMutated: nothing is emitted.

notes.title: The equals and hashCode contract
notes.html:
The idea. Hash-based collections (HashMap, HashSet, LinkedHashMap, Android's ArrayMap) first use hashCode() to jump to a bucket, then equals() inside the bucket. The two methods must agree, or the collection cannot find things.

The contract (inherited from Java).

  1. Reflexive: a == a.
  2. Symmetric: a == b implies b == a.
  3. Transitive: a == b and b == c imply a == c.
  4. Consistent: repeated calls give the same result while nothing relevant changes.
  5. a.equals(null) is false.
  6. If a == b then a.hashCode() == b.hashCode() (the reverse need not hold).

Overriding equals without hashCode. Two equal objects get different identity-based hash codes, so they usually land in different buckets:

class Point(val x: Int, val y: Int) {
    override fun equals(o: Any?) = o is Point && x == o.x && y == o.y   // no hashCode override
}
val s = hashSetOf(Point(1, 2))
s.contains(Point(1, 2))     // false (most of the time), looked in the wrong bucket

It sometimes passes, which makes it worse: with a small table two different hashes can map to the same bucket.

Inheritance breaks equals. The classic Point and ColorPoint: if Point.equals accepts any Point and ColorPoint.equals also compares colour, then point == colorPoint is true but colorPoint == point is false (symmetry broken). Using javaClass/getClass() equality instead fixes symmetry but breaks substitutability (a subclass instance is never equal to its parent). There is no perfect solution with concrete classes; the guidance is "favour composition" and the reason data classes are final. Lint/IDE inspection flags missing hashCode.

Industry usage. Room @Entity, DiffUtil, Set<Item> in selection state, caches keyed by request objects (OkHttp's HttpUrl, Glide's Key implementations such as ObjectKey define both methods carefully because they are cache keys).

Real-life picture. A library with a shelf code (hash) and a book title (equals). If two copies of the same book are given different shelf codes, the librarian searching shelf 7 never finds the copy filed on shelf 12.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "equal hash codes imply equal objects": collisions exist.
  • Writing hashCode from mutable fields and using the object as a key.
  • Fixing symmetry with instanceof in an open hierarchy and ignoring the Liskov consequences.

notes.title: Mutable data class as a hash key
notes.html:
The idea. hashCode() is computed from the current property values. If an object is stored in a HashMap/HashSet and then one of those properties changes, the object's hash changes, but the collection still has it in the old bucket. It is now unfindable.

data class Key(var id: Int)
val k = Key(1)
val set = hashSetOf(k)
k.id = 2
set.contains(k)        // false: looks in bucket for hash(2), the entry sits in bucket for hash(1)
set.remove(k)          // false: cannot remove it
set.size               // 1: it is still there, leaking
set.iterator().next()  // finds it (iteration walks all buckets)

Internals. HashMap stores each entry's hash at insertion; lookup computes hash(key), picks table[(n-1) & hash], then compares the stored hash and equals. After mutation the new hash picks another bucket, and even if it landed in the same bucket the stored hash would mismatch.

Android incident pattern (spot-the-bug). A multi-select feature stores HashMap<Item, Boolean> or HashSet<Item> of selected items where Item is a data class with var title/var isFavorite. After a rename or a favourite toggle the item "unselects itself", counts are off, "select all" leaves ghosts, and memory grows because removed entries stay. LeakCanary would not flag it (not a Context leak), you find it by heap-dumping the map and seeing size larger than visible items.

Fixes. Key by an immutable id (Set<Long> of ids, or Map<ItemId, ...>), make key classes fully val, or remove/re-insert around mutation. Compose's SnapshotStateList<Long> of selected ids is the idiomatic version.

Real-life picture. Filing a person's folder under the first letter of their surname; she gets married and changes surname; the folder stays in the old drawer, and a search under the new name finds nothing.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing data class makes the key safe: it only makes hashCode content-based.
  • Looking for the bug with contains and getting confused because iteration still finds the entry.
  • Using Item objects rather than their ids as keys in selection state.

notes.title: Arrays and body properties inside data classes
notes.html:
Arrays use identity equality. Array, IntArray, ByteArray do not override equals/hashCode for content, so a data class with an array property compares them by reference:

data class Packet(val bytes: ByteArray)
Packet(byteArrayOf(1)) == Packet(byteArrayOf(1))    // false, plus a compiler warning

IntelliJ/Kotlin warns "Property with 'Array' type in a 'data' class: it is recommended to override 'equals()' and 'hashCode()'". Fixes:

  1. Prefer List<Byte> (or a dedicated class) where size is moderate.
  2. Override both methods using contentEquals / contentHashCode() (the IDE generates this: if (!bytes.contentEquals(other.bytes)) return false).
  3. Use ByteString (Okio), which is value-comparable and immutable.

Body properties are invisible. A property declared inside the braces is excluded from all generated members.

data class Post(val id: Long, val text: String) {
    var liked: Boolean = false     // not in equals/hashCode/toString/copy
}

Classic UI incident. areContentsTheSame(old, new) = old == new in DiffUtil. The user taps the heart, the code does post.copy().also { it.liked = true } (or mutates liked), == says "equal", DiffUtil reports no change, and the heart never redraws ("like button does not update"). Same failure when copy() is used: copy does not carry body state either, so post.copy(text = "x") silently resets liked to false.

Fix. Put every property that affects UI or identity in the primary constructor; keep genuinely derived/cached values in the body deliberately and document it.

Industry examples. Network payloads (ByteArray for thumbnails, encrypted blobs) and Room entities with ByteArray blobs; Instagram-style feed items with isLiked or isSaved flags.

Real-life picture. A form with a sticky note stuck on the back. Photocopying the form (copy) and comparing forms (equals) ignore the note; if the note says "urgent", the copy is not urgent.

Common interview traps.

  • Expecting copy() to keep body-declared state.
  • Array equality in data classes used as map keys or compared in tests (assertEquals fails mysteriously).
  • Hiding a property in the body to "avoid noise in toString" and breaking DiffUtil.

notes.title: copy() is shallow
notes.html:
The idea. copy() builds a new object with the same property values, letting you change some. It is the standard way to update immutable state.

val old = User(1, "Asha", null)
val new = old.copy(name = "Asha K")        // id and email carried over

Mechanism. copy is a plain method (copy$default handles the default arguments with a bitmask) that calls the primary constructor. So init blocks and require(...) checks run again, and the new object is a different instance.

Shallow means shared inner objects. Properties are copied by reference:

data class Cart(val items: MutableList<String>)
val a = Cart(mutableListOf("book"))
val b = a.copy()
b.items.add("pen")
a.items            // [book, pen], same list instance

For a List<Item> typed as read-only the danger is lower but still real: the runtime object might be an ArrayList mutated elsewhere. Rules of thumb: expose List/Set/Map (read-only types), never keep a mutable collection inside a "value" object, replace rather than mutate (copy(items = items + "pen")).

Deep updates. Nested immutable models need chained copies (state.copy(profile = state.profile.copy(address = state.profile.address.copy(city = "Pune")))). Libraries such as Arrow Optics generate lenses to flatten this; with Compose, keep UI state flat.

Where it is used. MutableStateFlow.update { it.copy(isLoading = false) } in virtually every MVVM/MVI Android app (Google's Now in Android sample, Uber and Airbnb architecture talks), Redux-style reducers, Compose remember { mutableStateOf(State()) }.

Performance note. copy of a large object copies all references (cheap) but allocates; it is fine at human-event frequency, not in a per-frame animation loop.

Real-life picture. Photocopying a form and correcting one box on the copy. The original on the desk is untouched, but if the form says "see attached file", both copies point to the same attached file.

Common interview traps.

  • "copy() is a deep copy."
  • Mutating a list that a StateFlow already emitted: the "new" state equals the old one and nothing is emitted.
  • Forgetting that body properties are not copied.

notes.title: copy() bypassing invariants and copy visibility
notes.html:
The idea. A private constructor plus a factory function is the usual way to guarantee that an object is always valid (a normalised email, a non-negative amount). In a data class, the synthesised copy() used to be public even when the constructor was private, so anyone could build an invalid instance.

data class Email private constructor(val value: String) {
    companion object {
        fun of(raw: String): Email? =
            raw.trim().lowercase().takeIf { "@" in it }?.let(::Email)
    }
}
val e = Email.of("A@B.com")!!
val bad = e.copy(value = "not an email")    // compiled before the fix: validation in of() skipped

What changed (Kotlin 2.0.20 and later; confirm exact version flags in the release notes). The compiler warns when a data class with a non-public constructor exposes a public copy. Two annotations choose the behaviour explicitly:

  • @ConsistentCopyVisibility: copy (and the synthesised componentN are unaffected) gets the same visibility as the constructor. This is the intended future default.
  • @ExposedCopyVisibility: keep the old public copy, knowingly; suppresses the warning.

There is also the compiler option -Xconsistent-data-class-copy-visibility to opt in globally.

Design trade-off. If a type has real invariants, either (a) data class + private constructor + @ConsistentCopyVisibility + factory (and optionally a public copyWith... function that re-validates), or (b) a regular class with explicit equals/hashCode, or (c) a value class (@JvmInline value class Email private constructor(val value: String)), which has no copy. Mention binary compatibility: changing copy visibility in a published library is a breaking change for its callers.

Industry examples. Domain value types in banking and payments apps (Money, Iban, PhoneNumber), Stripe-style amount classes, validated form fields.

Real-life picture. A bank cheque book with a printed account name. The bank issues cheques only after verifying you. copy() was a photocopier next to the counter that let anyone make a new cheque without verification.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing private constructor is enough protection in a data class.
  • Saying the fix is private copy: you cannot declare copy yourself; use the annotations.
  • Forgetting init { require(...) } runs on copy (so validating in init is the simplest protection when you can).

notes.title: Destructuring and componentN
notes.html:
The idea. val (id, name) = user is shorthand that calls component1() and component2().

val (id, name) = user
// compiles to: val id = user.component1(); val name = user.component2()
for ((key, value) in map) { ... }          // Map.Entry has component1/2 as extension functions
val (quotient, remainder) = Pair(7 / 2, 7 % 2)

Rules. Components are positional, named component1..componentN, matching the order of the primary constructor. You can skip with _ (val (_, name) = user), and destructuring also works in lambda parameters (users.map { (id, name) -> ... }). Any class can support it by declaring operator fun componentN().

The risk. Order is the only link. If someone reorders constructor parameters (name before id), every destructuring site still compiles (both are String/Long... or both String) and silently swaps values. Adding a property at the front shifts everything. Data classes with two String fields (firstName, lastName) are especially dangerous. Public API destructuring also freezes your property order for binary compatibility.

Guidance used by teams. Destructure Pair, Triple, Map.Entry and short-lived local results; prefer named access (user.name) for domain models. Kotlin 2.x work on name-based destructuring is in progress/experimental (confirm in the release notes before relying on it).

Real-life picture. Seat numbers on a train ticket: "seat 1, seat 2". If the railway re-numbers the seats, everyone who memorised the number sits in the wrong place; a name card on the seat does not have that problem.

Common interview traps.

  • Thinking destructuring matches by name.
  • Reordering primary constructor parameters in a published data class.
  • Forgetting Pair/Triple generate component functions too (they are data classes).

notes.title: Data class inheritance limits
notes.html:
The idea. A data class is final: you cannot write open data class or extend one with another data class. The reason is the equals contract.

Why. Suppose data class Point(val x: Int, val y: Int) could be subclassed by data class ColorPoint(val x: Int, val y: Int, val color: String) : Point(x, y). Each generated equals checks other is ThisClass, so a Point would equal a ColorPoint in one direction but not the other (symmetry broken); copy on a ColorPoint through a Point reference would return the wrong type; componentN clash. Making them final removes the whole class of bugs.

What a data class may do.

  • Implement interfaces (including sealed interface), the standard way to model hierarchies: data class Success(...) : Result.
  • Extend an open or abstract class: data class Admin(val level: Int) : Person(). Generated members cover only the primary-constructor properties of the data class, not the parent's state. If the parent has a final equals/toString/hashCode, the data class does not generate that member (it uses the parent's); if the parent has open ones, the data class generates its own.
  • Supply default copy parameters, toString, etc. by writing them yourself: an explicit equals/hashCode/toString in the body suppresses generation of that member.

Alternatives. Composition (data class ColorPoint(val point: Point, val color: String)), sealed hierarchies of data classes, or interfaces carrying shared properties.

Industry usage. Result and UI state hierarchies (sealed interface UiState { data class Content(...) }), Room entities with a shared BaseEntity abstract class for id.

Real-life picture. Passport copies: you cannot create a "special passport" by stapling extras onto the real one and still pass it as a normal passport for comparison checks.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying a data class cannot extend anything.
  • Believing the parent's properties appear in the child's toString/equals.
  • Trying open data class (compile error: modifier not applicable).

notes.title: Cost of generated equals and hashCode
notes.html:
The idea. The generated methods touch every primary-constructor property, so their cost grows with class size and with the cost of nested equality. Usually negligible, occasionally a hot spot.

Where it shows up.

  • DiffUtil/ListAdapter/Compose LazyColumn diffs. areContentsTheSame runs equals for every compared pair on a background thread. A feed Post with 40 fields, nested lists of comments and a List<Image> makes each equals walk big graphs. Thousands of comparisons per update add up (Perfetto shows long DiffUtil.calculateDiff slices off the main thread, and jank if the result dispatch is heavy).
  • HashSet/HashMap with big keys. hashCode recomputes every time (no caching in a data class, unlike String). Looking up a key that holds a 10,000-element list hashes the whole list on every get.
  • Compose recomposition. Stable equals of large state objects on every frame.

Measure first. Use Android Studio CPU profiler / Perfetto / Macrobenchmark; then:

  1. Compare ids first: areItemsTheSame uses the id; areContentsTheSame only runs for matched items.
  2. Use a slim UI model (only fields displayed) mapped from the large network/domain model.
  3. Compare cheap fields first by writing equals yourself (version/updatedAt) when you own a monotonic version.
  4. Cache the hash for immutable keys (private val hash by lazy { ... } in body, or @Stable-annotated immutable state).
  5. Use ImmutableList (kotlinx.collections.immutable) or @Immutable for Compose stability so unchanged state is skipped without deep equality.

Real-life picture. Checking if two suitcases are identical by unpacking every item each time. Fast for a handbag, slow for a ship container; better to compare the baggage tag number first.

Common interview traps.

  • Optimising before profiling.
  • Computing hashCode of big mutable collections in keys.
  • Forgetting that equals on List is element-wise deep.

notes.title: Enum classes
notes.html:
The idea. An enum is a fixed set of named constants known at compile time (days of the week, order statuses, log levels). Each constant is a singleton instance of the enum class, created when the class is loaded.

enum class Status(val code: String) {
    PENDING("P"),
    SHIPPED("S") { override fun label() = "On the way" },   // per-constant body
    DELIVERED("D");
    open fun label() = name.lowercase().replaceFirstChar(Char::uppercase)
    fun isFinal() = this == DELIVERED
}

What the compiler makes (decompiled shape).

public enum Status {
    PENDING("P"), SHIPPED("S") { ... }, DELIVERED("D");     // each = public static final field
    private static final Status[] $VALUES = $values();       // private array of all constants
    private static final EnumEntries $ENTRIES = EnumEntriesKt.enumEntries($VALUES); // Kotlin 1.9+
    public static Status[] values() { return $VALUES.clone(); }   // a COPY each call
    public static Status valueOf(String name) { return (Status) Enum.valueOf(Status.class, name); }
    public static EnumEntries getEntries() { return $ENTRIES; }
}

An enum with a per-constant body gets an anonymous subclass (Status$2); constants without a body use the enum class itself. Every enum extends java.lang.Enum, which stores name and ordinal (8 bytes of fields plus the object header and its own fields, so each constant is a small object).

Capabilities. Constructor properties, methods, abstract members implemented per constant, interface implementation (enum class Op : (Int, Int) -> Int), companion objects, and use in when. Not allowed: extending another class or being extended; no new constants at runtime.

Industry use. Order status in Swiggy/Uber, Log.Priority, Android's own Lifecycle.State and Lifecycle.Event, Bitmap.Config, Retrofit HttpMethod, feature tiers.

Memory note. Android's guidance once discouraged enums (a few hundred bytes of dex/class overhead each); with R8 optimisations and enum unboxing (R8 can replace some enums with ints when it can prove it is safe, confirm per AGP version) this is no longer a general concern, but a library with 500 enum classes still costs dex size.

Real-life picture. The days-of-the-week wall chart: seven fixed slots, each slot a real thing you can point to, none can be added by customers.

Common interview traps.

  • "Enums are just integers": they are objects (R8 may optimise, not guaranteed).
  • Forgetting values() allocates (next section).
  • Trying to add a new constant at runtime or to subclass.

notes.title: entries, values, EnumMap and EnumSet
notes.html:
values() copies; entries does not. The decompiled values() ends with .clone() because the JVM cannot hand out the private array. Calling it in a hot loop (Status.values().forEach inside onBindViewHolder) allocates a new array every time. Kotlin 1.9 added Status.entries: an EnumEntries<Status>, an immutable List<Status> created once (the $ENTRIES field). It is stable from Kotlin 1.9 and cheaper; use it everywhere. It also works on Java enums (confirm the JDK requirement in the docs).

Status.entries.firstOrNull { it.code == stored }         // no array copy
Status.valueOf("SHIPPED")                                // throws IllegalArgumentException if unknown
Status.entries.associateBy { it.code }                   // build a lookup map once

EnumMap and EnumSet. Specialised java.util collections for enum keys.

  • EnumMap<K, V>: stores values in an Object[] indexed by ordinal(); lookup is an array index, no hashing, no collision, no entry objects, iteration in declaration order.
  • EnumSet<E>: a bitset. RegularEnumSet uses one long (up to 64 constants), JumboEnumSet uses a long[]. contains, add, union are bit operations.
val enabled = EnumSet.of(Feature.DARK_MODE, Feature.OFFLINE)
val pricePerPlan = EnumMap<Plan, Int>(Plan::class.java)

When to use. Small fixed key spaces with frequent lookups: feature flags, permission sets, per-state analytics counters, price tables, UI state maps. Kotlin's enumSetOf-style helpers are not in stdlib (use EnumSet.noneOf(...) / toCollection). Not worth it for two or three keys in cold code.

Real-life picture. EnumMap is a hotel key rack with one labelled hook per room: you go straight to the hook. A HashMap is a clerk computing a code from the room name and searching the bucket each time.

Common interview traps.

  • Using values() inside adapters/draw code.
  • Saying entries is a Kotlin-only feature (it also works with Java enums).
  • Relying on ordinal ordering across app versions (see persisting enums).

notes.title: Exhaustive when with enums
notes.html:
The idea. If every constant is handled, when needs no else, and the compiler can verify completeness.

fun label(s: Status): String = when (s) {          // expression: must be exhaustive
    Status.PENDING -> "Pending"
    Status.SHIPPED -> "Shipped"
    Status.DELIVERED -> "Delivered"
}

When the compiler forces it. Always for when used as an expression (assigned, returned, used as the last lambda value). Since Kotlin 1.7, non-exhaustive when statements on enum, sealed and Boolean subjects are an error (previously a warning).

Under the hood. The compiler emits a tableswitch on ordinal(), through a synthetic WhenMappings class holding an int[] indexed by the enum's ordinal (the mapping array is built at class init to survive reordering within the same compilation). An exhaustive expression without else gets a default branch that throws NoWhenBranchMatchedException (Kotlin) for a value the compiler did not know about.

Why seniors avoid else on enums. An else -> swallows every future constant: add REFUNDED and nothing warns you that this when silently takes the else path (wrong colour, wrong analytics, wrong business rule). With explicit branches, the compiler lists every place to update. Use else only when the default is truly semantic ("everything else is treated the same") and add a comment.

Library boundary. If the enum comes from a dependency compiled separately and gains a constant, your already-compiled when throws NoWhenBranchMatchedException at runtime (or IncompatibleClassChangeError in some shapes). This is also the server-enum problem: unknown values should map to UNKNOWN before they reach when.

Industry example. Android's Lifecycle.Event handling in LifecycleEventObserver, and AGP's own deprecation of when fallthrough warnings; Google's samples use exhaustive when on UiState.

Real-life picture. A kitchen order screen with one button per dish. A new dish appears; a screen that lists every dish shows an error until you map it, while a screen with an "everything else" button quietly sends it to the wrong station.

Common interview traps.

  • Adding else "just in case" and losing compiler help.
  • Believing exhaustiveness protects precompiled library callers.
  • Treating when statements as non-exhaustive (since 1.7 they are checked).

notes.title: Persisting enums: ordinal versus name versus code
notes.html:
The idea. Whatever you store (database, SharedPreferences/DataStore, JSON, Parcel, Intent) outlives the app version that wrote it. The representation you choose must survive source changes.

Stored value Breaks when
ordinal (0, 1, 2) you insert a constant in the middle, reorder, or sort alphabetically
name ("SHIPPED") you rename a constant (refactoring tool, R8 obfuscation if names are not kept)
your own stable code only if you reuse a code (policy: never reuse)

Migration under live traffic (scenario). A team stored ordinal in Room and in a server API. A new ON_HOLD was inserted before SHIPPED: after release, old rows silently change meaning (shipped orders appear as on hold, refunds issued wrongly), and Room does not complain. Recovery plan: (1) stop shipping changes that reorder, (2) add a new stable code column / field, populate it from the old ordering in a migration, (3) read both during a transition (new field preferred, old as fallback), (4) write both, (5) later remove the old one. Keep the old ordinal mapping in one explicit table in code, with a test that pins it (assertEquals(2, OldOrder.SHIPPED.legacyOrdinal)).

Parsing safely.

enum class Status(val code: String) {
    PENDING("P"), SHIPPED("S"), DELIVERED("D"), UNKNOWN("?");
    companion object {
        private val byCode = entries.associateBy { it.code }
        fun fromCode(c: String?) = byCode[c] ?: UNKNOWN
    }
}

Room: @TypeConverter using the code. Moshi: a custom adapter or @Json(name = "S") on constants with EnumJsonAdapter.create(Status::class.java).withUnknownFallback(UNKNOWN). kotlinx.serialization: @SerialName("S") plus coerceInputValues = true with a default value, or @JsonNames.

Unknown values from servers. Backends ship new values before apps update. valueOf throws IllegalArgumentException; Gson returns null for unknown enum names (surprise NPE later). Swiggy/Uber-style order and ride states always carry an UNKNOWN fallback with a generic UI ("Update the app for details").

Real-life picture. Restaurant bills that say "dish number 5". The owner inserts a new dish in the middle of the menu, and all old bills now mean something different. Writing the dish code (not the position) on the bill is stable.

Common interview traps.

  • Storing ordinal because it is "smaller": it is the one thing that must not be stored.
  • Relying on name while R8 can obfuscate enum names (keep rules or use explicit codes).
  • Letting Gson silently produce null for unknown enum strings.

notes.title: How an object declaration compiles
notes.html:
The idea. object Analytics { ... } declares a class that has exactly one instance, reachable by name. No getInstance() ceremony.

object Analytics {
    val sessionId = UUID.randomUUID().toString()
    fun log(e: String) { ... }
}

Decompiled shape.

public final class Analytics {
    public static final Analytics INSTANCE;
    private static final String sessionId;
    private Analytics() {}
    static {
        Analytics var0 = new Analytics();
        INSTANCE = var0;
        sessionId = UUID.randomUUID().toString();
    }
    public final void log(String e) {...}
}

Kotlin callers write Analytics.log(..); the compiler emits Analytics.INSTANCE.log(..). Java callers must write Analytics.INSTANCE.log(...), or use @JvmStatic to expose a real static method.

Initialization and thread safety. The singleton is created in the class's static initializer (<clinit>). The JVM/ART runs <clinit> once, lazily, the first time the class is actively used (first access of a static member or constructor). The class-initialization lock guarantees that exactly one thread runs it and other threads wait, which is why object is a thread-safe lazy singleton without synchronized (the "initialization-on-demand holder" idiom). Reading INSTANCE after init needs no lock. It is not initialized at app start unless something touches it.

Cycles. If object A initializer touches object B and B's initializer touches A, you can observe a half-initialized object (fields still null/0) because the same thread re-enters <clinit>. Another thread would deadlock. Keep initializers free of cross-object dependencies.

Object expressions are different. object : Runnable { ... } is an anonymous instance created each time the expression runs (see the nested/inner topic); object Name is the singleton declaration.

Industry usage. Utility holders (object Dispatchers-style constants), Logger, TimeProvider default implementations, Companion of every class, Retrofit service factory holders.

Real-life picture. A town has one fire station. Everyone calls it by name, nobody can build a second, and it opens the first time someone needs it.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying the object is created at app start or "eagerly on classload of the app".
  • Believing lazy is involved: it is plain JVM class-init semantics.
  • Forgetting Java sees .INSTANCE.

notes.title: Failures during object initialization
notes.html:
The idea. If code in an object's initializer throws, the class becomes permanently unusable in that process, and the error you see later is not the one that happened.

What the JVM/ART does.

  1. First access: <clinit> throws, e.g. FileNotFoundException. The runtime wraps it: java.lang.ExceptionInInitializerError (with the real exception as the cause). The class is marked "erroneous".
  2. Every later access (any thread, any code path): java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class com.app.Config. There is no new stack for the original failure.

Production incident pattern. object Config { val file = File(path).readText() } or object Crypto { val key = loadKeystoreKey() }. On one device model the keystore throws once at startup (low storage, KeyStoreException, OEM bug). Crashlytics shows one ExceptionInInitializerError (maybe filtered or lost in a non-fatal) and then thousands of NoClassDefFoundError across unrelated features; the issue title hides the root cause. Restarting the process is the only way to retry, so users see "crashes until I reinstall".

Prevention.

  • Keep object initializers trivial: constants, simple allocations.
  • Do risky I/O in an explicit fun init(): Result<...> or in a by lazy { } whose exception is not cached (lazy rethrows and, in default mode, tries again on the next access because the initializer did not complete).
  • Wrap in runCatching, log the original exception and fall back.
  • Look for the first ExceptionInInitializerError in Crashlytics breadcrumbs/logs or filter by "Caused by".

Reproduce. A unit test that touches the object after forcing the failing dependency; on JVM tests the first call yields ExceptionInInitializerError, the second NoClassDefFoundError.

Real-life picture. A fire station whose doors jam on opening day: the town can never use it, and every later caller just hears "station not available", with no hint of the original jam.

Common interview traps.

  • Hunting the NoClassDefFoundError as a missing dependency (R8/multidex) when it is a failed initializer.
  • Assuming lazy and object retry the same way (object never retries).
  • Doing network or disk I/O in an object initializer.

notes.title: Companion objects
notes.html:
The idea. Kotlin has no static keyword. A companion object is the object attached to a class that holds what Java would make static: factory functions, constants, loggers.

class Profile private constructor(val id: Long) {
    companion object {
        const val TAG = "Profile"                  // static final field on Profile
        @JvmField val EMPTY = Profile(0)           // static field, no getter
        @JvmStatic fun from(id: Long) = Profile(id)   // real static method
        fun fromJson(s: String) = Profile(s.toLong()) // instance method on Companion
    }
}

Decompiled shape.

public final class Profile {
    public static final Companion Companion = new Companion(null);   // static field holding the instance
    public static final String TAG = "Profile";
    public static final Profile EMPTY;
    public static final Profile from(long id) { return Companion.from(id); }   // from @JvmStatic
    public static final class Companion {
        public final Profile from(long id) {...}
        public final Profile fromJson(String s) {...}
        private Companion() {}
        public Companion(DefaultConstructorMarker m) { this(); }   // synthetic, so outer class can create it
    }
}

Initialization. The companion instance and its property initialisers run in the outer class's static initializer, i.e. when Profile is first loaded/touched, not when the companion is first used and not at app start. Companion state therefore starts on the first access of the outer class, with the same thread-safety guarantees as object.

Java access. Without annotations, Java writes Profile.Companion.fromJson(s). @JvmStatic adds a real static method (Profile.from(1)), @JvmField and const expose fields as statics. const works only for primitives and String and is inlined at call sites.

Differences.

companion object top-level function/val plain object
Can access outer's private members yes no no
Tied to a class name yes (Profile.from) no (fromJson in file) own name
Can implement interfaces and be passed as value yes (Profile as a factory object) no yes
Java callers Companion unless annotated FileKt.fromJson .INSTANCE

Android patterns. companion object { const val ARG_ID = "id"; fun newInstance(id: Long) = Fragment().apply {...} }, private const val TAG, Intent factories (MainActivity.start(context)). Prefer top-level private const val TAG for constants to avoid creating a companion class for one constant (each companion adds a class to dex).

Real-life picture. The reception desk of a company: not a regular employee, but belongs to the building and handles "how do I get in" for everyone.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying companion members are Java statics: only with @JvmStatic/@JvmField/const.
  • Treating companion as eager init at app start.
  • Forgetting const only works for primitives and String.

notes.title: data object
notes.html:
The idea. In a sealed hierarchy, cases without data are written as object Loading : UiState. A plain object has a poor toString() (UiState$Loading@6f2b958e), identity-only equals, and surprises when copied through serialization. Kotlin 1.9 added the data modifier for objects.

sealed interface UiState {
    data object Loading : UiState
    data class Content(val items: List<Item>) : UiState
    data class Error(val message: String) : UiState
}
println(UiState.Loading)     // "Loading"  (not UiState$Loading@6f2b958e)

What it generates.

  • toString() returns the object's simple name.
  • equals() is true for any instance of the same object type, and hashCode() is consistent with it, so even a second instance created by reflection or deserialization is equal to the original. A plain object equals only itself by identity.
  • It does not generate copy() or componentN() (nothing to copy).
  • It stays a singleton (INSTANCE).

Why it matters. Logs, Crashlytics custom keys and breadcrumbs print readable state; Compose previews and test failure messages say Loading instead of a hash; assertEquals(UiState.Loading, state) works even if the instance came through a serializer or process boundary; when with UiState.Loading -> compiles to an equality check, so equal-but-distinct instances still match, while for a plain object such an instance would fall through to the exhaustive-when exception.

Version note. Stable in Kotlin 1.9. For Serializable objects, confirm whether the compiler adds readResolve for you in your version; otherwise declare it yourself (next section).

Industry use. Every MVVM/MVI sealed UiState, Event, Result hierarchy in modern apps (Google's Now in Android, Slack/Uber style architectures), navigation Route objects (data object Home : Route with type-safe Navigation Compose 2.8 and kotlinx.serialization).

Real-life picture. A road sign that says "STOP" versus a blank board with a serial number: same sign, but one tells you what it is.

Common interview traps.

  • Calling data object a data class: no copy, no components.
  • Leaving object in sealed hierarchies on Kotlin 1.9 and above (lint suggests data object).
  • Assuming === and == on data object mean the same thing after deserialization.

notes.title: object singleton versus DI singleton
notes.html:
The idea. Both give "one instance", but with different lifetimes, wiring and testability.

Kotlin object Hilt/Dagger @Singleton (or Koin single)
Created on first class access (lazy, JVM class init) when first injected / component built
Lifetime the whole process, forever the owning component (Application, Activity, ViewModel scope, custom)
Dependencies cannot take constructor parameters constructor injection
Testing global state leaks between tests, hard to swap replace with fake in a test module
Multiple instances impossible possible per scope (multi-account, per-user graph)
Configuration at runtime static init order problems explicit order via graph

Ambiguous requirement (scenario). "We need one SessionManager." Question back to product: per process, per user, or per account? If a user can log out and another log in, an object with state keeps the previous user's data until manually cleared (privacy bug, stale caches). A scoped DI binding tied to a user component is discarded with the session.

Guidance.

  • object for stateless helpers, constants, markers (data object), and pure default implementations.
  • DI for repositories, API clients, databases, anything with dependencies or state.
  • Mark Hilt @Singleton classes carefully: they live until process death and hold memory.

Industry examples. Hilt's @Singleton on OkHttpClient, Room database, Retrofit service; ViewModel scoped bindings (@ViewModelScoped); apps with multiple accounts (Gmail, Slack) build a per-account graph; object-based service locators are what Square/Google move away from for testability.

Real-life picture. A single town fire station (object) versus a fire brigade assigned to each district by the city council (DI): the council can reassign, replace and train them separately.

Common interview traps.

  • Using object with lateinit var context (Context leak and hidden init order).
  • Believing @Singleton means "JVM singleton": it is singleton per component instance.
  • Forgetting that state in object survives across tests and across user sessions.

notes.title: Singleton identity across serialization
notes.html:
The idea. A singleton only stays a singleton if nothing can create a second instance. Serialization frameworks create objects without calling your code.

How it breaks.

  • Java serialization / Serializable through Intents, Bundles or saved state: deserialization allocates a new instance of the object class, so value === Loading becomes false even though it prints the same. == on plain object is also identity, so when (state) { Loading -> ... } falls through.
  • Gson: serializes a Kotlin object as {} and deserializes to a new instance (using Unsafe), not INSTANCE.
  • Parcelable: generated Parcelable for an object creates a new instance unless the CREATOR returns INSTANCE.

Symptoms. After process death and restore, a screen stuck in a "loading" or "empty" branch; NoWhenBranchMatchedException in an exhaustive when over a sealed type restored from a Bundle; works in unit tests, fails after a restore. A post-incident review typically traces it to Serializable sealed state saved in onSaveInstanceState.

Fixes.

  1. data object so equals is value-like and still correct for a second instance.
  2. For Java-serialized singletons, implement private fun readResolve(): Any = INSTANCE (the JVM's serialization hook that substitutes the canonical instance).
  3. Use a Kotlin-aware serializer: kotlinx.serialization supports object and data object and returns the same instance; Moshi and Gson need adapters.
  4. Don't put UI state in Bundles at all: restore from SavedStateHandle using primitives/ids and rebuild state.
  5. Prefer enums for singletons you must serialize: the JVM guarantees enum identity through serialization.

Real-life picture. A club with exactly one president's badge. Photocopying the badge during a restore (deserialization) gives you a lookalike that the door guard rejects, unless the guard compares names instead of badges (data object equality).

Common interview traps.

  • Assuming object identity survives Parcel/Serializable.
  • Using === in when branches against an object restored from outside the process.
  • Forgetting that enums are the safe singleton for serialization.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
Data classes. Generate equals, hashCode, toString, componentN, copy from primary-constructor properties only; body properties and Array contents (identity) are traps; never use mutable data classes as map keys; final (no inheritance between data classes), may implement interfaces; cost scales with fields, so compare ids first and keep UI models small.

Equality. == is equals (null-safe), === is identity. Contract: reflexive, symmetric, transitive, consistent, null-false, equal objects have equal hash codes. Overriding one without the other loses entries in hash collections. Inheritance breaks symmetry.

copy(). Shallow, runs the constructor and init, drops body state, can bypass factory validation when the constructor is private (Kotlin 2.0.20+ warns; @ConsistentCopyVisibility / @ExposedCopyVisibility). Destructuring is positional and fragile.

Enums. Singleton constants with properties, methods, interfaces; values() clones, entries does not; EnumMap (array by ordinal) and EnumSet (bitmask) are the fast collections; when should be exhaustive without else; persist a stable code, never ordinal, and always map unknown server values to UNKNOWN.

Objects. object compiles to a class with static INSTANCE built in <clinit>: lazy and thread-safe through JVM class initialisation. A throwing initialiser yields ExceptionInInitializerError, then NoClassDefFoundError forever. Companion objects are an instance held in a static Companion field, initialised with the outer class; use @JvmStatic, @JvmField, const for Java. data object gives readable toString and value-like equality. DI singletons beat object for stateful services; serialization can duplicate singletons unless you use readResolve, data object or a Kotlin-aware serializer.

Interview one-liners.

  • "Only the primary constructor counts for equals, hashCode, toString, copy."
  • "Equal objects must have equal hash codes; keys must be immutable."
  • "copy is shallow and may sidestep your factory's validation."
  • "entries over values(); store a stable code, never the ordinal."
  • "object init is class init: lazy, thread-safe, and one failure poisons it forever."
  • "Serialization can mint a second singleton."

questions.promptHtml: What does the compiler generate for a data class, and which properties take part in it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It's the most common Kotlin warm-up question, and a quick way to find out who knows the "primary constructor only" rule and who just says "it generates getters".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: For a data class the compiler generates equals(), hashCode(), toString(), copy() and component1()..componentN(). All of them use only the properties declared in the primary constructor. A property declared in the class body is invisible to every generated member. If I write equals, hashCode or toString myself, or a supertype has a final version, the compiler doesn't generate that member. copy and componentN can't be hand-written.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A data class is an ordinary final JVM class plus generated members. The requirements are:

  • The primary constructor has at least one parameter, and every parameter is val or var.
  • The class can't be abstract, open, sealed or inner.
  • It can extend a class and implement interfaces (allowed since Kotlin 1.1).

Here is what you get for data class User(val id: Long, val name: String?), roughly as decompiled:

Member Generated behavior
toString() "User(id=1, name=Ann)": class name plus primary-ctor props in declaration order
hashCode() result = id.hashCode(); result = 31 * result + (name?.hashCode() ?: 0)
equals(other) this === other → true; other !is User → false; then compares each prop (Intrinsics.areEqual for references, Long/Int compared directly, Float/Double via compare)
copy(id = this.id, name = this.name) new instance; default args are the current values
component1(), component2() return id, name in order, for destructuring

Two runtime details a senior candidate should know:

  1. The generated equals short-circuits on identity (===) first. If both sides are the same instance, the comparison costs O(1).
  2. For Double/Float properties the generated equals compares with java.lang.Double.compare-style total ordering. Two Point(Double.NaN) instances are therefore equal, while Point(0.0) != Point(-0.0). That differs from 0.0 == -0.0 on primitives. Confirm this with Kotlin Bytecode → Decompile for your compiler version.

The generated members aren't cached. hashCode() is recomputed on every call, and it walks nested lists and maps fully.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
data class User(val id: Long, val name: String) {
    var lastSeen: Long = 0L // body property: NOT in equals/hashCode/toString/copy
}

fun main() {
    val a = User(1, "Ann").apply { lastSeen = 100 }
    val b = User(1, "Ann").apply { lastSeen = 999 }
    println(a == b)            // true: lastSeen ignored
    println(a)                 // User(id=1, name=Ann): no lastSeen
    println(a.copy().lastSeen) // 0: copy() only passes ctor params
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming body properties take part in equality. They are silently ignored, including by copy(), so the value is reset to its initializer.
  • Assuming you can override copy() or componentN() by hand. Explicit implementations are compile errors.
  • Putting Array properties in a data class: equality on them is by reference. See Q049.
  • Treating toString() as safe to log. It prints every primary property, including tokens and PII.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do I exclude a field from equality? → Move it to the class body, or override equals/hashCode by hand. The body approach also excludes it from copy, which may be a bug.
  2. Can a data class have no properties? → No, it needs at least one ctor parameter. Use data object for the stateless case (Q047).
  3. What happens if a superclass declares final override fun toString()? → The data class inherits it and the compiler doesn't generate one. The same applies to equals and hashCode.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer lists the five members. The senior answer adds the primary-constructor-only rule and its consequences for copy(), the identity short-circuit, the Double total-order semantics, the fact that hashCode is uncached, and the PII risk of the generated toString.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A login data class Session(val user: String, val token: String) ended up in Crashlytics logs through string templates. The fix was overriding toString() to redact the token.

questions.promptHtml: What's the difference between == and === in Kotlin, and what does a == b compile to?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks the Java-to-Kotlin mental model shift, and whether you know how nulls and floating point behave under each operator.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: == is structural equality. It compiles to a?.equals(b) ?: (b === null), so it's null-safe and calls equals. === is referential equality: same object or not, and it never calls equals. One trap: for Float/Double statically typed as such, == follows IEEE 754 (NaN != NaN, 0.0 == -0.0). When the static type is Any or generic, == falls back to equals(), which has the opposite results.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
a == b    ->  if (a == null) b == null else a.equals(b)   // Intrinsics.areEqual(a, b)
a != b    ->  !(a == b)
a === b   ->  reference comparison (JVM if_acmpeq), no method call
  • equals can't be overloaded as an operator. You override open operator fun equals(other: Any?): Boolean from Any.
  • x == null compiles to a plain null check, so it has no cost.
  • For primitive-typed values (Int, Long) == compares values directly. === on them is deprecated (warning "Identity equality for arguments of types Int and Int is deprecated") because the result depends on boxing. The Integer cache trap is covered in chunk K1b.
  • Floating point depends on the static type:
Static type NaN == NaN 0.0 == -0.0
Double / Double? false (IEEE 754) true
Any, Comparable<Double>, T true (Double.equals) false

This matters in generic code. A List<Double>.contains(Double.NaN) returns true, while Double.NaN == Double.NaN returns false.

  • For data object and enums, == and === give the same result in normal code. Docs still advise == for data objects because reflection or serialization can create a second instance (Q047).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val a = "hello"
val b = StringBuilder("hel").append("lo").toString()
println(a == b)   // true  - equals()
println(a === b)  // false - different String objects

val x: Double = Double.NaN
val y: Any = Double.NaN
println(x == x)        // false - IEEE
println(y == y)        // true  - Double.equals
println(listOf(x).contains(Double.NaN)) // true - uses equals

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using === on strings because "it worked in tests". Literals are interned, but runtime-built strings aren't.
  • Expecting == on two Arrays to compare contents. It compares references, so use contentEquals.
  • Forgetting that == on a type whose equals is broken inherits the bug. == is only as good as equals.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is a == b safe if a is null? → Yes, it compiles to a null check before calling equals.
  2. When would you deliberately use ===? → Identity checks: "did this list instance change" shortcuts, sentinels, DiffUtil.areItemsTheSame on stable cached instances. Never for value comparison.
  3. Why does setOf(0.0).contains(-0.0) return false? → Set uses Double.equals/hashCode, which separates 0.0 and -0.0, while 0.0 == -0.0 on primitives is true.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "== is equals, === is reference". The senior answer adds the exact null-safe expansion, the static-type dependency for floating point, the identity deprecation for primitives, and when identity checks are a legitimate optimization.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A price-dedupe step keyed Map<Any, ...> by boxed Double treated -0.0 and 0.0 as different keys, and users saw two "free" rows. The fix was normalizing to BigDecimal/cents.

questions.promptHtml: State the equals/hashCode contract. What goes wrong in a HashMap if I override equals but not hashCode, and how does inheritance break equals?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Glassdoor senior lists literally include "What can go wrong with equals() and hashCode()?". It separates people who've debugged a hash collection from people who memorized a definition.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: equals must be reflexive, symmetric, transitive, consistent and return false for null. Equal objects must have equal hash codes, though unequal objects may collide. If I override equals without hashCode, two equal objects land in different buckets, so map[key] misses and a Set holds duplicates. With inheritance, an is-based equals in a base class plus an extra field in a subclass breaks symmetry. That's why data classes are final and compare with other !is Type.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
How HashMap.get(k) works:

h = spread(k.hashCode())            // 1. pick bucket by hash
bucket = table[h & (n-1)]
for node in bucket:                 // 2. within bucket:
    if node.hash == h && (node.key === k || node.key.equals(k)) return node.value

The hash picks the bucket first, so equals only ever runs between keys whose hashes match. Here's what each kind of violation does:

Violation Symptom
equals overridden, hashCode not (identity hash) map[User(1)] returns null for an equal key; Set dedupe fails
hashCode uses a mutable field, mutated after insert entry becomes unreachable ("lost" key), memory leak in caches
equals asymmetric (a == b but b != a) list.contains result depends on argument order; distinct() nondeterministic
hashCode constant (e.g. = 1) still correct, but every key lands in one bucket. Java 8+ treeifies a bucket at 8 entries (once table capacity ≥ 64); lookups are roughly O(log n) only if keys are Comparable, otherwise they degrade toward O(n)

The inheritance problem:

open class Point(val x: Int, val y: Int) {
    override fun equals(other: Any?) = other is Point && x == other.x && y == other.y
    override fun hashCode() = 31 * x + y
}
class ColorPoint(x: Int, y: Int, val color: Int) : Point(x, y) {
    override fun equals(other: Any?) =
        other is ColorPoint && super.equals(other) && color == other.color
}
// Point(1,2) == ColorPoint(1,2,RED)  -> true
// ColorPoint(1,2,RED) == Point(1,2)  -> false  (symmetry broken)

There are three ways out:

  • Make the class final, as data classes are.
  • Compare javaClass == other.javaClass. This keeps symmetry but violates Liskov, since a subclass is never equal to its parent.
  • Use composition instead of inheritance.

Floating-point fields: use compare/toBits semantics, as the generated data class code does (Q036).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class Key(val id: Int) {
    override fun equals(other: Any?) = other is Key && other.id == id
    // BUG: no hashCode override -> identity hash
}

fun main() {
    val m = hashMapOf(Key(1) to "a")
    println(m[Key(1)])   // null (almost always): different bucket
}

// Correct, manual version for a non-data class:
class GoodKey(val id: Int, val tag: String) {
    override fun equals(other: Any?): Boolean {
        if (this === other) return true
        if (other !is GoodKey) return false
        return id == other.id && tag == other.tag
    }
    override fun hashCode(): Int = 31 * id + tag.hashCode()
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Writing fun equals(other: Key), an overload instead of an override. Kotlin requires override with Any?, which catches this, but Java code doesn't.
  • Including lazily computed or mutable fields in hashCode.
  • Making equals depend on something like Context or time.
  • Relying on "the test passed". With an identity hash, a lookup occasionally hits by chance when both keys end up in the same bucket.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can two unequal objects have the same hash? → Yes, that's a collision. It's legal, it just costs performance.
  2. Why 31 in hashCode? → It's an odd prime, and 31 * i == (i << 5) - i is cheap. It's a convention, not a correctness requirement.
  3. How does a data class avoid the symmetry problem? → It's final, and its equals checks other !is Self. If you extend an open base with its own equals, you can still create asymmetry, so keep the base's equals abstract or final.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer recites "override both". The senior answer explains bucket lookup mechanics, why mutable fields in hash codes lose entries, the subclass symmetry break, and the javaClass vs is trade-off.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An image cache keyed by a hand-written RequestKey that lacked hashCode had a 0% hit rate. Memory looked like a leak and network was 3x the expected volume. The one-line fix was converting it to a data class.

questions.promptHtml: Is a data class copy() deep or shallow? What are the consequences, and what changed about copy() visibility in Kotlin 2.x?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Immutable UI state is built on copy(). Shallow-copy bugs show up as "UI not updating" and "state mutated from somewhere else".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: copy() is shallow. It calls the primary constructor with the same references for every property I don't override, so a MutableList or nested mutable object is shared between the original and the copy. That's fine and fast if everything nested is immutable, and dangerous if anything is mutable. On visibility: before Kotlin 2.0.20, copy() was always public, even with a private constructor, which let callers bypass validation. 2.0.20 started a deprecation cycle so that copy matches the constructor's visibility. You opt in now with @ConsistentCopyVisibility or -Xconsistent-data-class-copy-visibility.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
val a = State(items = mutableListOf(1,2), user = User("x"))
val b = a.copy(loading = true)

a ──► State ─┬─ items ──► [ArrayList 1,2] ◄──┐
             └─ user  ──► User("x")  ◄──┐   │
b ──► State ─┬─ items ──────────────────┼───┘   (same list)
             └─ user  ──────────────────┘       (same User)
  • Cost: copy() is one allocation plus field copies, and doesn't recurse. That's why immutable-state architectures are cheap.
  • Danger: b.items.add(3) also changes a. Anything comparing old to new, such as DiffUtil, StateFlow's distinct check or Compose skipping, now sees "old == new" because both point at the mutated list.
  • Deep copy isn't provided. You copy nested parts explicitly: copy(items = items.toList()), write per-type copy functions, or better, make nested types immutable (List, kotlinx.collections.immutable per chunk K7) so sharing is safe.
  • Body properties aren't passed to copy() (Q036), so their initializer values come back.
  • The copy() visibility change (verify the exact version for your toolchain against KT-11914):
    • 2.0.20 added warnings when a data class with a non-public constructor exposes copy.
    • Later 2.x releases escalate this to an error, then flip the default.
    • @ConsistentCopyVisibility opts in early: copy gets the constructor's visibility.
    • @ExposedCopyVisibility keeps the old public binary signature during migration.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Validated value via private constructor
@ConsistentCopyVisibility // Kotlin 2.0.20+: copy() becomes private like the ctor
data class Email private constructor(val value: String) {
    companion object {
        fun of(raw: String): Email? =
            raw.trim().takeIf { "@" in it }?.let(::Email)
    }
}
// Without the annotation (pre-change default), callers could do:
// Email.of("a@b.c")!!.copy(value = "not-an-email")  // validation bypassed

// Shallow copy trap
data class Cart(val items: MutableList<String>)
fun main() {
    val a = Cart(mutableListOf("apple"))
    val b = a.copy()
    b.items += "pear"
    println(a.items) // [apple, pear]
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using copy() as a "clone" before mutating nested state.
  • Declaring val items: MutableList<T> in UI state. val only freezes the reference, not the contents.
  • Assuming a private constructor is enough for invariants on pre-2.x behavior when copy is public.
  • Running heavy validation in init and forgetting that copy() also runs init. It does, because it calls the constructor, so that's actually good for invariants but costs CPU in hot copy loops.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does copy() run init blocks? → Yes, it's a constructor call.
  2. How would you deep-copy a graph-shaped state? → Usually you don't. You make it immutable and structurally share it. If you really must, write explicit mapping or serialize/deserialize, which is slow.
  3. Why not make copy() deep by default? → Cost would become proportional to graph size, cycles would recurse forever, and identity-based shortcuts like === in equals and DiffUtil identity checks would be lost. Structural sharing is the point.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "shallow, so nested objects are shared". The senior answer adds the aliasing consequences for diffing and state flows, the immutability-instead-of-deep-copy design choice, copy running init, and the 2.0.20+ copy visibility migration with its annotations.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A UiState(filters: MutableSet<Filter>) was "copied", then mutated, then emitted. StateFlow saw an equal value and dropped it, so the filter chip toggled only visually on the next unrelated emission.

questions.promptHtml: How does destructuring like val (id, name) = user work, and what's the risk of using it on data classes?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks whether you know destructuring is positional sugar over componentN(), and whether you've seen the refactoring hazard.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Destructuring compiles to calls to component1(), component2() and so on. Those are operator functions that a data class generates in primary-constructor order. Any class can opt in by declaring operator fun componentN(). The risk is that it's positional, not by name. If someone reorders two same-typed properties in the constructor, every destructuring site silently swaps values and still compiles.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• val (a, b) = x compiles to val a = x.component1(); val b = x.component2().
  • Where it's used:
    • Lambdas: map.forEach { (k, v) -> }. Note that { (k, v) -> } is one destructured param, while { k, v -> } is two params.
    • for ((i, v) in list.withIndex()).
    • Pair and Triple.
    • Map.Entry, through stdlib extension component1/2.
  • Use _ to skip: val (_, name) = user. The compiler doesn't call component1() for _.
  • The hazard:
data class Range(val start: Int, val end: Int)      // v1
val (s, e) = range
data class Range(val end: Int, val start: Int)      // v2 refactor: compiles, swaps silently
  • Kotlin has been working on name-based destructuring as an alternative. Check the current "What's new" for its status in your Kotlin 2.x version, and don't assume it's stable.
  • Cost: no allocation for data classes. For Pair/Triple the cost is the object itself.
  • Adding a property in the middle of a public data class changes componentN and copy signatures. That's a binary-incompatible change for library consumers, which is one reason library authors avoid public data classes.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
data class User(val id: Long, val name: String, val email: String)

fun render(u: User) {
    val (id, name) = u            // component1(), component2()
    val (_, _, email) = u         // only component3() called
    println("$id $name $email")
}

class Size(val w: Int, val h: Int) {
    operator fun component1() = w
    operator fun component2() = h
}
val (w, h) = Size(10, 20)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Destructuring wide domain objects with same-typed fields (String id/name/email). Positional bugs won't be caught.
  • Confusing { (a, b) -> } with { a, b -> } in lambdas.
  • Assuming destructuring matches variable names to property names. It doesn't: val (name, id) = user gives name = id.
  • Exposing a public data class in an SDK and then appending or reordering properties, which breaks consumers' binaries.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can I destructure a non-data class? → Yes, if it declares operator fun componentN(), either as members or extensions.
  2. How many components are generated? → One per primary-ctor property. There's no artificial cap, unlike the stdlib's 5-component List destructuring extensions.
  3. Why do some style guides ban destructuring of domain models? → It's positional coupling with no compiler protection. They allow it only for Pair and map entries, where position is the semantics.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer knows the syntax. The senior answer explains componentN lowering, the silent-swap refactor hazard, the binary compatibility cost of public data classes, and team guidelines on where destructuring is allowed.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team swapped lat/lng order in a LatLng-like data class during a cleanup. A val (lat, lng) = pos in the map renderer put markers in the ocean for one release.

questions.promptHtml: Why can't a data class be open? What can a data class inherit from, and what happens to the generated members when it does?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It probes whether you understand that the language restriction exists to protect the equals contract. It's also the basis of modeling sealed state hierarchies correctly.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A data class is implicitly final and can't be open, abstract, sealed or inner. A subclass adding fields would break equals symmetry and make copy() return the wrong type. A data class can extend an open or abstract class and implement interfaces. That's the standard sealed interface UiState + data class Success(...) : UiState pattern. If the parent has final equals/hashCode/toString, the data class uses the parent's versions. If the parent declares open properties, the data class can override them in its constructor.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Why it's final:

  • copy() is fun copy(...): Self. A subclass Sub : Data would inherit a copy() returning Data, losing Sub's fields.
  • Generated equals uses other !is Data. A subclass with extra state would be equal to the parent but not vice versa, which is the symmetry break from Q038.

What's allowed:

Supertype member Effect on generated code
abstract val x / open val x data class override val x in ctor; included in equals
final override fun equals in parent not generated; parent's used (possibly ignoring child props!)
open equals in parent generated override replaces it
final fun componentN with incompatible type compile error
parent ctor properties not redeclared NOT part of data class equals

That last row is a real trap:

abstract class Entity(val id: Long)
data class Note(val text: String, val ownerId: Long) : Entity(ownerId) // id not in equals unless redeclared

The usual recommended shape: put the hierarchy root in a sealed interface (or an abstract class with no state), with data classes or data objects as leaves. Keep shared state in each leaf's constructor, or in a wrapper, rather than in a stateful base class. The sealed vs enum trade-off is covered in chunk K2b.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
sealed interface Shape { val area: Double }

data class Circle(val r: Double) : Shape {
    override val area get() = Math.PI * r * r // body getter, not part of equals - fine, it's derived
}
data class Rect(val w: Double, val h: Double) : Shape {
    override val area get() = w * h
}

abstract class Base(open val id: String)
data class Item(override val id: String, val title: String) : Base(id) // id included in equals

// data class Sub(val x: Int) : Item("a", "b")   // error: Item is final

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using a stateful base class (BaseModel(id, createdAt)) for data classes. Base fields are excluded from equality and copy() can't change them.
  • Writing final override fun equals in a shared base "for logging". It silently disables value equality in every child.
  • Using the all-open compiler plugin (Spring/JPA style) on data classes. It makes them open, so the guarantees disappear. That plugin belongs to chunk K8.
  • Expecting copy() to exist on the interface type. It doesn't, because each leaf has its own signature.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can a data class implement Comparable? → Yes. Keep compareTo consistent with equals or TreeSet will dedupe differently from HashSet.
  2. Can a data class be sealed? → No. A sealed parent with data class children is the idiom.
  3. How do you share a copy-like operation across sealed leaves? → An abstract function on the sealed type (fun withLoading(): UiState) implemented in each leaf with its own copy.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "data classes are final". The senior answer explains why (copy return type, equals symmetry), lists exactly which parent members suppress generation, flags the "base ctor field not in equals" trap, and recommends stateless sealed roots.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A BaseMessage(id, timestamp) parent with data class children made two different messages with the same text compare equal. DiffUtil merged rows in the chat list.

questions.promptHtml: What can a Kotlin enum class contain? Show constructor properties, per-constant bodies and interface implementation. What does each compile to?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It's a fundamentals check, and it sets up follow-ups on allocation, R8 and when an enum should be a sealed type instead.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An enum is a class with a fixed set of instances created once in its static initializer. It can have constructor properties, methods, abstract members that each constant implements in its own body, and it can implement interfaces. Every constant gets name and ordinal. The class gets valueOf(String), values() and, since Kotlin 1.9, entries. A constant with a body compiles to an anonymous subclass. That affects javaClass, so use declaringJavaClass instead.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Bytecode: final class Color extends java.lang.Enum<Color>. It has a public static final Color RED, a private $VALUES array, and since 1.9-compiled code, an $ENTRIES field. <clinit> constructs every constant in order.
  • If any constant has a body, the enum class becomes abstract-ish and the constant is an instance of a synthetic subclass like Color$RED. Then RED.javaClass != Color::class.java. Use RED.declaringJavaClass (Kotlin 1.7+) or Java's declaringClass.
  • valueOf("PURPLE") throws IllegalArgumentException. There's no null-returning variant built in, so use entries.firstOrNull { it.name == s }.
  • ordinal is the declaration position. It isn't stable across reordering, so never persist it (Q051).
  • Enums are Comparable by ordinal, and Serializable through java.lang.Enum. Java serialization of enums is by name and always yields the canonical instance, unlike object (Q055).
  • Android cost: each constant is an object plus static init. Modern R8 can "unbox" simple enums to ints in release builds. Whether a given enum qualifies depends on usage (reflection, valueOf, bodies, being used as a generic type argument) and on the R8 version. The old "never use enums on Android" advice dates from Dalvik and no longer applies.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
interface Pricing { fun price(base: Int): Int }

enum class Tier(val label: String) : Pricing {
    FREE("Free") {
        override fun price(base: Int) = 0
    },
    PRO("Pro") {
        override fun price(base: Int) = base
    },
    TEAM("Team") {
        override fun price(base: Int) = base * 5
        override fun badge() = "★"
    };                                   // semicolon required before members

    open fun badge(): String = ""

    companion object {
        fun fromLabel(l: String): Tier? = entries.firstOrNull { it.label == l }
    }
}

fun main() {
    println(Tier.TEAM.price(10))                       // 50
    println(Tier.PRO.javaClass == Tier::class.java)    // false - anonymous subclass
    println(Tier.PRO.declaringJavaClass == Tier::class.java) // true
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting the ; after the last constant when the enum has members.
  • Using valueOf on server strings without handling unknown values. It throws in production when the backend adds a value.
  • Comparing javaClass for enums with bodies, or using it in reflection-based serializers.
  • Putting mutable state in enum constants. It's global, shared and survives across tests.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can enums have abstract properties? → Yes, each constant must override them in its body, or declare them through the constructor.
  2. Can an enum extend a class? → No, it already extends java.lang.Enum. It can implement interfaces.
  3. When does enum <clinit> run, and can it fail? → On first use of the enum class. An exception there causes ExceptionInInitializerError and then NoClassDefFoundError, the same mechanics as object (Q052).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer shows a property and a when. The senior answer knows constants with bodies become subclasses (declaringJavaClass), that valueOf throws, that ordinal is unstable, and the modern R8 unboxing reality instead of the outdated "avoid enums" advice.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A backend added a new Tier value. Tier.valueOf(json.tier) in a hand-written parser crashed 100% of cold starts for users on that tier until a hotfix shipped.

questions.promptHtml: Why did Kotlin add Enum.entries to replace values()? And when would you use EnumMap/EnumSet instead of HashMap/HashSet keyed by an enum?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks whether you track language evolution (1.9) and understand allocation in hot paths, not just the syntax.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: values() returns a fresh clone of the internal array on every call, because arrays are mutable and the JVM can't hand out the shared one. Calling it in a loop or in onBind allocates every time. entries, stable since Kotlin 1.9.0, returns a pre-built immutable EnumEntries<E>, a List<E>, so it costs nothing per call and works with collection APIs. Kotlin 2.0.0 added the generic enumEntries<T>() to replace enumValues<T>() for the same reason. EnumMap and EnumSet index by ordinal into an array or bit vector, which is faster and smaller than hashing. I use them for any enum-keyed lookup.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
values():   return $VALUES.clone()          // new Array<Color>(n) per call
entries:    return $ENTRIES                  // one EnumEntries list, created once
  • entries arrived as experimental in 1.8.20 and became stable in 1.9.0. When an enum was compiled by an older compiler or by Java, Kotlin builds the entries list through a synthetic mapping holder, so it still works for Java enums.
  • EnumEntries<E> is an immutable List<E>, so entries.indexOf(x), entries.random() and entries.associateWith { } all just work.
