  • enumEntries<T>() (2.0.0) is a reified generic accessor for writing generic helpers such as inline fun <reified T : Enum<T>> parse(s: String).

Comparing enum-keyed collections:

Structure Storage get/contains Notes
HashMap<Color, V> buckets + Node objects hash + equals ordering by hash (or insertion for LinkedHashMap)
EnumMap<Color, V> Array<Any?> sized to entries vals[key.ordinal] iterates in declaration order, no Node allocation, null keys rejected
EnumSet<Color> one long bitmask (≤64 constants, RegularEnumSet) or long[] (JumboEnumSet) bit test allOf, noneOf, range, complementOf

These are Java collections. Kotlin's mapOf(...)/setOf(...) return LinkedHashMap/LinkedHashSet and don't specialize enums automatically.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import java.util.EnumMap
import java.util.EnumSet
import kotlin.enums.enumEntries

enum class Perm { READ, WRITE, DELETE, ADMIN }

// Allocates a new Array on every call
fun slowHasAdmin(names: List<String>) =
    names.any { n -> Perm.values().any { it.name == n } }

// Zero-alloc lookup structure built once
private val byName: Map<String, Perm> = Perm.entries.associateBy { it.name }
fun parse(n: String): Perm? = byName[n]

inline fun <reified T : Enum<T>> safeValueOf(s: String): T? =
    enumEntries<T>().firstOrNull { it.name == s } // Kotlin 2.0.0+

val counters = EnumMap<Perm, Int>(Perm::class.java).apply {
    Perm.entries.forEach { put(it, 0) }
}
val granted: EnumSet<Perm> = EnumSet.of(Perm.READ, Perm.WRITE)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling values() inside onBindViewHolder, a Compose recomposition or a parser loop. It's harmless once, garbage-churning at 60 fps.
  • Assuming entries is a snapshot copy you can mutate. It's immutable, so toMutableList() it if needed.
  • Using EnumMap with an empty Map source (EnumMap(emptyMap())). That throws, because there's no class token to infer. Pass Class<E>.
  • Persisting ordinal because EnumMap uses it internally. Ordinal is fine in memory and wrong on disk (Q051).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is values() deprecated? → No, it's still supported. The IDE suggests entries (an inspection in recent IntelliJ/AS) and enumEntries<T>() over enumValues<T>().
  2. How big is an EnumSet of 10 constants? → One object plus one long field: 10 bits used.
  3. Does R8 enum unboxing still work if I use EnumMap? → Probably not for that enum. EnumMap needs the real Class object, which counts as an escape. In practice the allocation saved by EnumMap matters more than unboxing. Measure if it matters.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "entries is the new values()". The senior answer explains the clone-per-call mechanics, gives the versions (1.8.20 experimental, 1.9.0 stable, enumEntries 2.0.0), shows the build-once lookup map pattern, and picks EnumMap/EnumSet with an understanding of their ordinal-indexed storage.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A profiler allocation trace on a chat list showed thousands of MessageType[] allocations per second from MessageType.values()[viewType] in onCreateViewHolder. Switching to entries[viewType] removed them.

questions.promptHtml: When does the compiler force a when on an enum to be exhaustive, and why do senior engineers avoid else branches on enums?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Exhaustiveness is your main compile-time safety net when the domain changes. This checks whether you design for "the next constant someone adds".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A when used as an expression must be exhaustive. Since Kotlin 1.7, a when statement whose subject is an enum, sealed type or Boolean must also be exhaustive (it was a warning in 1.6). I list every constant and skip else. Then adding a constant breaks the build at every place that needs a decision, instead of silently falling into a default branch. The exception is enums owned by another module or the server, where new values can arrive at runtime without a recompile.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Compilation: when (color) over an enum compiles to a tableswitch on a synthetic WhenMappings array. That array maps the runtime ordinal to the switch index, so it's robust to reordering in separately compiled code.
  • An exhaustive when without else gets a hidden default branch that throws NoWhenBranchMatchedException. That can actually fire when:
    • an enum from another module (an AAR or library) gains a constant and your code isn't recompiled, a binary-compat drift;
    • a value is obtained through reflection or deserialization tricks.
  • Where else is right:
    • Mapping enums from a different module whose evolution you don't control, where a graceful fallback beats a crash.
    • Large enums where most constants share behavior, such as an analytics event type. Even then, consider grouping through a property on the enum.
Without else:     add Tier.ENTERPRISE  ──► compile error in 14 places ──► each one decided
With else:        add Tier.ENTERPRISE  ──► compiles ──► ENTERPRISE users get FREE behavior
  • Guard conditions in when branches (is X if cond ->) appeared as a preview in Kotlin 2.1. Their per-version status belongs to chunk K8. A guarded branch doesn't count toward exhaustiveness on its own.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
enum class Tier { FREE, PRO, TEAM }

fun limit(t: Tier): Int = when (t) {   // expression: must be exhaustive
    Tier.FREE -> 1
    Tier.PRO -> 10
    Tier.TEAM -> 100
}                                       // no else: adding a constant = compile error

fun log(t: Tier) {
    when (t) {                          // statement: also must be exhaustive since Kotlin 1.7
        Tier.FREE -> println("free")
        Tier.PRO, Tier.TEAM -> println("paid")
    }
}

// Risky: future constants silently become "free"
fun badLimit(t: Tier) = when (t) {
    Tier.PRO -> 10
    Tier.TEAM -> 100
    else -> 1
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Adding else -> throw IllegalStateException() "for safety". You lose the compile-time check and keep the crash.
  • Assuming exhaustiveness protects you against server-provided values. It doesn't, because deserialization decides those (Q051).
  • Forgetting that when (x) { A -> ...; B -> ... } with a nullable subject Tier? needs a null -> branch.
  • Using when on ordinal ints and losing all checking.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What's NoWhenBranchMatchedException? → The implicit default for exhaustive when without else. Seeing it in Crashlytics usually means a binary mismatch with a library enum.
  2. How do you force exhaustiveness on a statement before 1.7? → Assign it (val _ = when ...) or use an .exhaustive extension trick: val <T> T.exhaustive get() = this.
  3. Enums vs sealed for this? → Both get exhaustiveness. Sealed adds per-case data. That's chunk K2b's topic.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "expression when must be exhaustive". The senior answer gives the 1.7 statement rule, explains WhenMappings and NoWhenBranchMatchedException, and treats "no else" as a deliberate change-propagation tool, with a different policy for enums from external modules.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team added Tier.STUDENT. A when with else -> FREE_LIMITS in the paywall gave paying students free limits for two weeks before a support ticket found it. Removing else showed six more sites needing a decision.

questions.promptHtml: How does a Kotlin object compile? Is it thread-safe, when exactly is it initialized, and what happens if its initialization throws?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Singletons are everywhere in Android codebases. Seniors are expected to reason about the JVM/ART class-initialization model, startup cost and failure modes, not only "it's a singleton".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An object compiles to a final class with a private constructor and a public static final INSTANCE field assigned in its static initializer <clinit>. It's lazy because the JVM and ART initialize a class on first active use, such as accessing INSTANCE or a static member. It's thread-safe because class initialization runs under a per-class init lock (JLS 12.4.2). Other threads block until it finishes, with no double-checked locking needed. If <clinit> throws, the first caller gets ExceptionInInitializerError and the class is marked erroneous. Every later access then throws NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class X for the life of the process.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
object Analytics { val queue = ArrayDeque<String>(); fun track(e: String) { queue += e } }

decompiles to roughly:

public final class Analytics {
    public static final Analytics INSTANCE;
    private static final ArrayDeque queue;        // object property backing fields are static
    private Analytics() {}
    static { INSTANCE = new Analytics(); queue = new ArrayDeque(); }   // <clinit>
    public final ArrayDeque getQueue() { return queue; }
    public final void track(String e) { ... }
}
// Kotlin call site:  Analytics.track("x")  ->  Analytics.INSTANCE.track("x")

Initialization triggers include accessing INSTANCE, any static field that isn't a compile-time constant, a static method, or a subclass's initialization. const val is inlined at call sites and doesn't trigger init. Loading a class (for example during verification) isn't the same as initializing it.

The class-init state machine:

not initialized ──first use──► in progress (owner thread T1; others wait on init lock)
          ├─ success ──► initialized (fast path forever)
          └─ throws  ──► ERRONEOUS: T1 gets ExceptionInInitializerError(cause)
                         everyone later gets NoClassDefFoundError (no cause chain!)

Edge cases that bite:

  1. Recursive init in the same thread. If <clinit> of A touches A again, directly or via B, the same thread sees a partially initialized class (INSTANCE still null) with no error. That leads to NPEs inside object members.
  2. Cross-thread init deadlock. T1 initializes A, which needs B, while T2 initializes B, which needs A. Both wait forever on each other's init lock. On Android this looks like an ANR whose main thread is stuck in <clinit>.
  3. Main-thread cost. The first access pays the full <clinit>. If that reads SharedPreferences or parses JSON, the cost lands on whatever thread touched it first, often main during startup.
  4. The process is the scope. An object lives until process death. It isn't reset by Activity recreation, and it's re-created after process death with fresh state.

Object expressions (object : Runnable {}) are different. They're anonymous class instances created eagerly where written, a new instance each time, and not singletons.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Risky: fallible IO in <clinit>
object Config {
    val json: String = java.io.File("/data/cfg.json").readText() // throws -> class permanently broken
}

// Safer: keep init trivial; do fallible work lazily with a fallback
object SafeConfig {
    @Volatile private var cached: String? = null
    fun json(load: () -> String): String =
        cached ?: runCatching(load).getOrDefault("{}").also { cached = it }
}

runCatching is acceptable here only because this isn't a coroutine. See the cancellation chunk for why it's dangerous in suspend code.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Believing object initializes "at app start". It initializes on first use, and that's usually good.
  • Debugging NoClassDefFoundError as a multidex or R8 problem when the real cause is the earlier ExceptionInInitializerError. Look for the first occurrence in the session logs.
  • Holding an Activity/View in an object property, which leaks it for the process lifetime. Use applicationContext.
  • Mutable global state in objects, which makes unit tests order-dependent (Q054).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Do I need by lazy inside an object for thread-safety? → Not for the object itself. lazy is useful to defer one expensive property beyond the object's init.
  2. How do you make object members callable as true Java statics? → @JvmStatic/@JvmField/const. Interop details are in chunk K8.
  3. Can ART initialize my class before first use? → ART may pre-initialize classes in boot or app images only when their initializers are side-effect-free. Your semantics shouldn't depend on timing either way. Treat it as "first use".

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "object = thread-safe lazy singleton". The senior answer describes INSTANCE/<clinit>, the JVM init lock, the erroneous state that turns one exception into NoClassDefFoundError forever, recursive and cross-thread init hazards, and keeping <clinit> trivial.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A crash cluster titled NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class FeatureFlags was 40x larger than its real root cause, a single ExceptionInInitializerError per process from corrupted prefs. Full analysis in Q052.

questions.promptHtml: What is a companion object at the bytecode level, when is it initialized, and how is it different from a top-level declaration or a plain object?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Companion objects are the default place for factories, constants and loggers. Misunderstanding them causes interop surprises and hidden startup costs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A companion compiles to a nested class Outer$Companion plus a public static final Companion field on Outer. Backing fields of companion properties are actually private static fields on Outer, accessed through instance getters on Companion. It's initialized in Outer's static initializer, so it initializes when Outer is first used, including the first Outer() construction. That's Java static-init semantics. Unlike a top-level function, it can implement interfaces, be passed as a value and receive extension functions. A top-level declaration is cheaper and simpler when you don't need any of that.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
class Repo private constructor(val name: String) {
    companion object Factory : (String) -> Repo {
        const val MAX = 10                 // inlined at call sites
        val DEFAULT = Repo("default")      // private static field on Repo, init in Repo.<clinit>
        override fun invoke(name: String) = Repo(name)
        @JvmStatic fun create() = Repo("x") // also emits static Repo.create() delegating to Factory
    }
}
class Repo {
    public static final Repo.Factory Factory;     // the companion instance
    private static final Repo DEFAULT;            // companion val backing field lives HERE
    static { Factory = new Factory(null); DEFAULT = new Repo("default"); }
    public static final class Factory implements Function1<String, Repo> {
        public final Repo getDEFAULT() { return Repo.DEFAULT; }
        ...
    }
}

Consequences:

  • Calling the first Repo(...) runs Repo.<clinit>, so heavy companion vals, such as a Regex compile or JSON parse, are paid at first construction, whether or not you touch them.
  • Java callers write Repo.Factory.create() (or Repo.Companion.x() when unnamed) unless @JvmStatic/@JvmField/const is used. Chunk K8 covers those annotations in depth.
  • Kotlin access Repo.DEFAULT goes through Factory.getDEFAULT(), an extra call R8 usually inlines.
Choice Use when
top-level private const val / fun file-scoped helpers and constants: cheapest, no class instance needed
companion factory needing the private ctor, constants tied to the type, implementing an interface (e.g. Parcelable.Creator-like, serializer()), extensions on Type.Companion
separate object independent singleton with its own lifecycle and lazy init

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class Logger private constructor(val tag: String) {
    companion object {
        private val cache = HashMap<String, Logger>()  // in Logger.<clinit>
        fun of(tag: String) = cache.getOrPut(tag) { Logger(tag) } // not thread-safe: shortcut for main-thread-only use
    }
}

// Trap: costly companion init paid at first Logger construction even if unused
class Parser {
    companion object { val BIG_REGEX = Regex("""(?:[a-z0-9!#$%&'*+/=?^_`{|}~-]+)+@.+""") }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Treating companion as "static" and dumping unrelated helpers into it. Top-level functions are idiomatic.
  • Heavy work in companion property initializers. It runs when the outer class initializes, possibly on main during first inflation.
  • Thinking a companion is lazy separately from its outer class. It isn't, because its fields live in Outer.<clinit>.
  • Putting mutable state in a companion. It's still global state, shared across all instances and tests.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can a class have two companions? → No, one per class. You can add any number of nested objects.
  2. Why can kotlinx.serialization call User.serializer()? → The plugin generates it on the companion. Extensions on Companion also enable that call syntax.
  3. const val vs val in a companion? → const is a compile-time constant inlined into callers, so changing it requires recompiling consumers. Plain val is a static field read through a getter. Chunk K6 owns the details.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "companion is like static". The senior answer describes the static field on the outer class plus the nested class, the fact that init happens with the outer class (startup cost), Java call syntax without annotations, and when a top-level declaration or separate object is the better choice.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A ViewHolder class had a companion val building a large DateTimeFormatter map. That cost 30 ms on the main thread at first bind in a cold-start Perfetto trace. Moving it to a lazily initialized top-level val deferred it off the critical path.

questions.promptHtml: What is a data object, what exactly does it generate, and why should sealed-state singletons like Loading be data objects rather than plain objects?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It's a recent language feature (stable in 1.9.0) that shows whether you keep current. It also has a non-obvious equality nuance that matters for serialization and process death.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A data object is a singleton that generates toString(), which returns just the name (Loading instead of Loading@1b6d3586), plus equals() and hashCode() that treat any instance of that type as equal. It doesn't generate copy() or componentN(), since there are no properties, and you can't override its equals/hashCode. It went from preview in 1.8.20 to stable in 1.9.0. For sealed hierarchies it gives readable logs and test diffs, and stays correct even if reflection or serialization creates a second instance. The docs say to compare data objects with ==, never ===.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
plain object data object
toString() Loading@6d06d69c Loading
equals() identity (from Any) other is Loading (type-based)
hashCode() identity hash constant per type
copy, componentN no no
custom equals/hashCode allowed not allowed

Why type-based equality matters: a singleton's single instance is a convention the JVM doesn't enforce. A second instance can appear through:

  • java.io.Serializable deserialization without readResolve(). The compiler doesn't add it automatically, which is why IntelliJ has an inspection "Serializable object must implement readResolve". Verify with javap on your version.
  • Reflection or Unsafe allocation by reflective JSON libraries such as Gson.
  • Two class loaders in tests or plugins.

With a plain object, state == Loading is then false and when (state) { Loading -> } misses, because when with a value branch uses equality. With data object, equality survives. is Loading checks work for both. kotlinx.serialization handles objects by returning the existing instance, so it's not the culprit.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import kotlinx.serialization.Serializable

sealed interface UiState {
    data object Loading : UiState
    data object Empty : UiState
    data class Content(val items: List<String>) : UiState
    data class Error(val message: String) : UiState
}

fun render(s: UiState) = when (s) {
    UiState.Loading -> "spinner"        // equality check -> robust with data object
    UiState.Empty -> "empty"
    is UiState.Content -> "list ${s.items.size}"
    is UiState.Error -> "error ${s.message}"
}

// Navigation 2.8+ type-safe routes commonly use serializable data objects
@Serializable data object HomeRoute
@Serializable data class DetailRoute(val id: String)

fun main() {
    println(UiState.Loading)   // "Loading" - good for logs and test failure messages
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using === with data objects in new code. The docs explicitly advise ==.
  • Expecting data object to make Java-serialized singletons identical. Equality is fixed, identity isn't. Add readResolve if identity matters.
  • Converting a stateful object (a cache or manager) to data object "for nicer logs". Its equality semantics are meant for value-like singletons.
  • Leaving object Loading in sealed hierarchies, so test failures print expected Loading@1a2b but was Loading@3c4d.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can a data object have properties? → It can declare body properties, but they aren't part of toString/equals. Stateful data objects are a smell.
  2. Is data object binary compatible with object? → Callers still access INSTANCE, but you add or alter toString/equals/hashCode. Behavior changes for anyone relying on identity equality or the old toString format.
  3. How does data object relate to enum? → An enum is a closed set of instances of one type. A data object is one instance of its own type, usually a leaf of a sealed hierarchy next to data classes carrying data. The enum vs sealed choice is in chunk K2b.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "it gives a nice toString". The senior answer covers type-based equals and hashCode, the absence of copy and componentN, the prohibition on overriding, the 1.8.20 to 1.9.0 timeline, == vs === guidance, and the deserialization/reflection second-instance problem that makes it more correct, not just prettier.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: After process-death restore through a Java-Serializable saved state, object Loading came back as a new instance and when fell through, leaving a blank screen. Switching to data object fixed the equality branch. Full story in Q055.

questions.subtopic: Mutable data class as hash key
questions.contextHtml:
A download manager in a 1.2M-DAU podcast app shows a "N downloads active" badge. After the last release, about 6% of users report the badge stuck at "1" or "2" with nothing downloading, and heap dumps from internal testers show DownloadTask objects accumulating (~4k per long session). The team suspects a threading issue because progress comes from Dispatchers.IO. The code (simplified, assume single-threaded access for now):

data class DownloadTask(
    val episodeId: String,
    var progress: Int = 0,
    var state: State = State.QUEUED
)
enum class State { QUEUED, RUNNING, DONE }

class DownloadTracker {
    private val active = mutableSetOf<DownloadTask>()   // LinkedHashSet
    val activeCount: Int get() = active.size

    fun start(task: DownloadTask) { task.state = State.RUNNING; active += task }
    fun onProgress(task: DownloadTask, p: Int) { task.progress = p }
    fun finish(task: DownloadTask) {
        task.state = State.DONE
        val removed = active.remove(task)
        Log.d("DL", "finish ${task.episodeId} removed=$removed")   // logs removed=false
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: Find the bug, explain it mechanically, and fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "It's a race condition, wrap it in synchronized or use ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet()." That doesn't change the outcome, because even single-threaded code reproduces it. A weaker answer still: "Use a List instead," which hides the problem with O(n) removes but keeps identity confusion.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does it reproduce with a single download on a single thread? It does, which rules out the race. Is the same DownloadTask instance passed to start and finish? Yes. Is removed=false logged every time or only sometimes? Every time progress changed.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Make the badge count derive from authoritative storage, either the DB rows with state = RUNNING or WorkManager's work infos, not from this set. Ship that as a hotfix while the real fix lands.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) A mutable property included in hashCode, so the element sits in the wrong bucket after mutation. (b) Two different instances for the same episode, so equality depends on progress. (c) A race on a non-thread-safe set. That one is real, but secondary.
  4. How I'd verify each: A unit test: add, mutate progress, assert contains. It fails deterministically. Log task.hashCode() at start and at finish to see it change. Use a LeakCanary/heap dump to confirm the retained tasks are referenced only by active.
  5. Root cause: progress and state are primary-constructor vars, so they're part of the generated hashCode. start sets state = RUNNING before inserting, so the element is stored in the bucket for hash(RUNNING, 0). Then onProgress changes progress and finish sets DONE, so remove computes a different hash, looks in a different bucket and returns false. The element is now unreachable through hash lookups but still referenced. That gives a stuck count and a memory leak. equals would match, but HashMap never gets as far as calling it.
  6. Fix: Short-term: key the collection by the immutable identity. 
    data class DownloadTask(val episodeId: String, val progress: Int = 0, val state: State = State.QUEUED)

class DownloadTracker {
    private val active = LinkedHashMap<String, DownloadTask>()  // key = immutable id
    val activeCount: Int get() = active.size
    fun start(t: DownloadTask) { active[t.episodeId] = t.copy(state = State.RUNNING) }
    fun onProgress(id: String, p: Int) { active[id]?.let { active[id] = it.copy(progress = p) } }
    fun finish(id: String) { active.remove(id) }
}
    Long-term: model the state as immutable values flowing through a StateFlow<Map<String, DownloadTask>> owned by one confined writer. The confinement techniques are in chunk C8.
  7. Prevention:
    • Review checklist: no var in primary constructors of types used as keys or in sets.
    • A custom lint/detekt rule flagging data class with var ctor params.
    • A unit test for "mutate then remove".
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I wouldn't override hashCode to only use episodeId while keeping a value-based equals. That's legal per the contract but surprising, and two "different" tasks would collide. I'd also skip a synchronized wrapper as the fix. It addresses a different, real problem and leaves this one.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if DownloadTask were a normal class (no data)? → Identity hash and identity equals, so mutation wouldn't break the set. Value semantics bring the requirement of immutability.
  • Would iterating and removing through an iterator work? → Yes. iterator.remove() removes the node it's on without rehashing the key, which is why "it works when I clear via loop" can mislead.
  • Same bug with HashMap keys? → Identical. Any hash-based structure, including distinct(), groupBy keys and Compose key()s used in maps.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team saw a "zombie upload" badge that only cleared on app restart. The heap showed 3k upload tasks held by a HashSet. One var retries in a data class constructor, bumped after insertion, was the whole incident.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Blames threading only. Can't explain why remove returns false.
  • Hire: Identifies the mutable property in hashCode, explains buckets, fixes it with an immutable key.
  • Strong hire: Notes that state changes before insertion and again after, explains the unreachable-but-referenced leak, makes the badge derive from source of truth, and adds a lint rule and immutable state flow design.

questions.subtopic: Data class with arrays and body properties
questions.contextHtml:
A gallery screen (300 to 800 photos, mid-range devices like a Moto G, 60 Hz) uses ListAdapter. Since a "performance" refactor that started storing thumbnails as bytes, every DB emission (about every 2 s while syncing) makes all visible thumbnails flicker. Profiler shows onBindViewHolder running for every row on each emission, and long-pressing to select an item doesn't show the checkmark until you scroll away and back. Red herring: the team also upgraded RecyclerView to 1.3.x in the same release.

data class PhotoItem(
    val id: Long,
    val thumb: ByteArray,          // decoded from DB blob on each emission
    val takenAt: Long
) {
    var isSelected: Boolean = false
}

object PhotoDiff : DiffUtil.ItemCallback<PhotoItem>() {
    override fun areItemsTheSame(o: PhotoItem, n: PhotoItem) = o.id == n.id
    override fun areContentsTheSame(o: PhotoItem, n: PhotoItem) = o == n
}

// ViewModel, on long-press:
fun toggle(id: Long) {
    val list = _items.value
    list.first { it.id == id }.isSelected = !list.first { it.id == id }.isSelected
    _items.value = list.map { it }   // "new list" so StateFlow emits
}
questions.promptHtml: Explain both symptoms from the code alone, and give the fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Roll back the RecyclerView upgrade," or "Call notifyDataSetChanged() after toggling." The first chases the red herring. The second guarantees a full rebind, which makes the flicker worse.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Did the flicker start exactly with the ByteArray change? That's a git bisect. Does each emission create new ByteArray objects? Yes, because they're decoded from the blob per query. Is the selection state persisted or in-memory only?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Revert to loading thumbnails by URI/key through the image loader, which caches them. That's a quick, safe rollback of the "optimization".
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) ByteArray uses reference equality in generated equals, so contents are never "the same". (b) isSelected is a body property, so it's excluded from equals, and it's mutated in place on a shared instance. (c) The RecyclerView upgrade changed animation behavior. Unlikely, since the code alone explains everything.
  4. How I'd verify each: A unit test: PhotoItem(1, byteArrayOf(1), 0) == PhotoItem(1, byteArrayOf(1), 0) is false. Note the IDE warning "Property with 'Array' type in a 'data' class" on that line. Log areContentsTheSame results: always false on sync and always true on toggle. Count binds per emission in Android Studio's profiler or with a counter.
  5. Root cause:
    • Flicker: generated equals compares thumb with Intrinsics.areEqual, which is reference equality for arrays. Every emission decodes new arrays, so all 300+ items differ, DiffUtil dispatches change payloads for every visible row, and the default change animation cross-fades them. That's the flicker. hashCode uses the array's identity hash too, and toString prints [B@1f2e3d.
    • Selection: isSelected is declared in the body, so it's not in equals. Worse, toggle mutates the existing instance shared by the old list that the adapter holds and the new list. DiffUtil compares the object with itself (o === n), finds contents equal, and nothing rebinds. The checkmark only appears when the row is re-bound for another reason, such as scrolling.
  6. Fix: 
    data class PhotoItem(
    val id: Long,
    val thumbKey: String,       // URI/cache key; image loader handles bytes and caching
    val takenAt: Long,
    val isSelected: Boolean = false
)

fun toggle(id: Long) {
    _items.update { list -> list.map { if (it.id == id) it.copy(isSelected = !it.isSelected) else it } }
}
    If bytes truly must live in the model, override equals/hashCode with thumb.contentEquals(other.thumb) / thumb.contentHashCode(). Note that this costs O(bytes) per diff, which is another reason to prefer a key or content hash.
  7. Prevention:
    • Enforce the IDE inspection for array properties in data classes as an error in CI (detekt has comparable rules).
    • Make UI models fully immutable, with no body vars.
    • Add a unit test for the DiffUtil callback.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why): I wouldn't keep the bytes and override equals with contentEquals as the main fix. A 20 KB thumbnail times 300 rows is about 6 MB compared per emission. I'd also avoid notifyDataSetChanged() and setHasStableIds hacks, which mask the model bug.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Would List<Byte> instead of ByteArray fix equality? → Yes, List.equals is structural, but it boxes every byte. Terrible for memory.
  • Does StateFlow even emit after the in-place toggle? → list.map { it } is a new list, but it's equals to the old one because the elements are the same mutated instances. So StateFlow's equality conflation may drop it entirely. The mechanics are in chunk F2a.
  • Why did areItemsTheSame still work? → It compares id: Long, a primitive, so value equality.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "store thumbnails in Room to avoid disk reads" PR made a 500-row list rebind on every sync tick. Battery stats flagged the screen at 2x CPU. The diff was the one-line ByteArray field.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Blames the RecyclerView version or suggests notifyDataSetChanged.
  • Hire: Explains array reference equality and the body-property exclusion, and moves isSelected into the constructor.
  • Strong hire: Also explains the shared-instance mutation making old === new, questions storing bytes in UI models, quantifies diff cost, and adds lint/tests.

questions.contextHtml:
A wallet app (2.5M MAU) models money as a validated value, and also ships the type in a small public SDK used by 3 partner apps:

data class Amount private constructor(val cents: Long, val currency: String) {
    companion object {
        fun of(cents: Long, currency: String): Amount? =
            if (cents >= 0 && currency.length == 3) Amount(cents, currency) else null
    }
}
// somewhere in refunds:
val net = original.copy(cents = original.cents - fee.cents)

The backend reports 0.3% of refund requests arriving with negative amounts (about 900/day), which it rejects. That leads to support tickets and some "pending forever" refunds. At the same time, the team is upgrading Kotlin 1.9.24 → 2.x. The build now shows warnings that the non-public primary constructor is exposed through the generated copy(), at 41 call sites across 9 modules. One engineer proposes suppressing the warnings to unblock the upgrade.
questions.promptHtml: What's the root cause, how do you fix it, and how do you roll out the copy() visibility change without breaking partner apps?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a check before calling the API," or "suppress the warning, it's just a warning." Both leave the type's invariant breakable from anywhere. The second also walks into an error once a later Kotlin release escalates the warning.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Are partners calling copy() on Amount? That decides whether this is a binary-breaking change for them.
    • Is a negative Amount ever legitimate, for example a debit or adjustment? That decides between modeling it as a separate type and loosening the invariant.
    • What Kotlin version will partners compile against?
    • Do we have server-side validation as the real trust boundary? We do, and that's why it's rejected instead of paid.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix the refund path so it computes through a validating function and surfaces "fee exceeds amount" to the user. The backend keeps rejecting, which is the correct trust boundary. The client fix is UX, not security.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    • (a) copy() is public despite the private constructor, so any caller can create an invalid Amount. This is a known pre-2.x behavior and the subject of the deprecation.
    • (b) The fee is in a different currency, so the subtraction is semantically wrong. Worth checking, since it's a separate bug.
    • (c) An overflow or rounding issue. Unlikely with Long cents.
  4. How I'd verify each:
    • Grep for .copy( on Amount. The new compiler warnings conveniently list them.
    • Run a unit test: Amount.of(100, "USD")!!.copy(cents = -1) succeeds today.
    • Use server logs to correlate negative amounts with the fee > amount cases, and check currency mismatches.
  5. Root cause: Before the Kotlin 2.x change, the generated copy() of a data class is always public and calls the private constructor directly. Validation lived only in the of() factory, so copy() skipped it. The private constructor gave a false sense of encapsulation.
  6. Fix: Short-term, put the invariant in the type itself. init runs on copy() too, because copy is a constructor call. 
    @ConsistentCopyVisibility   // Kotlin 2.0.20+: copy() gets the constructor's (private) visibility
data class Amount private constructor(val cents: Long, val currency: String) {
    init {
        require(cents >= 0) { "negative amount" }        // last line of defence
        require(currency.length == 3) { "bad currency" }
    }
    fun minus(other: Amount): Amount? =
        if (other.currency != currency || other.cents > cents) null
        else Amount(cents - other.cents, currency)       // private ctor usable inside
    companion object {
        fun of(cents: Long, currency: String): Amount? =
            if (cents >= 0 && currency.length == 3) Amount(cents, currency) else null
    }
}
    Then replace the 41 copy sites with domain operations (minus, withCurrency) that return Amount? or a Result. Long-term, plan the SDK rollout:
    • In the public SDK module, first ship a release with @ExposedCopyVisibility. It keeps copy public at the binary level, so partners' compiled code still links, and it adds the replacement APIs.
    • Announce the deprecation.
    • In the next major version, switch to @ConsistentCopyVisibility.
    • Making copy private in a published artifact causes NoSuchMethodError/IllegalAccessError in partner apps compiled against the old binary, so it must be a major version. Run a binary-compatibility validator (e.g. the Kotlin binary-compatibility-validator Gradle plugin) to make the change visible in review.
  7. Prevention:
    • Turn on -Xconsistent-data-class-copy-visibility for internal modules so the new behavior applies everywhere.
    • Add a review checklist item: "a private ctor on a data class requires @ConsistentCopyVisibility and an init invariant."
    • Add a unit test asserting invalid construction throws.
    • Keep server-side validation as the real guard.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why):
    • I wouldn't suppress warnings. That postpones a guaranteed future break.
    • Throwing in init crashes on invalid input, so I keep it as an assertion behind validated factories, not as the primary validation path.
    • A @JvmInline value class with an init check is an alternative for single-field values. Its boxing and interop rules are covered in chunk K2b.
    • I wouldn't drop data entirely. equals/hashCode/toString are still valuable for money.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Does @ConsistentCopyVisibility make copy unavailable inside the class? → No. It's private, so the class's own members can still use it.
  • Why not make the constructor internal instead? → Then copy becomes internal too under the new rules, which helps across modules but still lets every caller in the same module bypass of().
  • What if partners use Java? → They call amount.copy(...), the same binary method. The same break applies, so the major-version rule holds.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "validated" email type with a private constructor ended up holding "" in production profiles. A copy(value = input.trim()) in a form mapper had bypassed the factory for two years. The fix was an init invariant plus making copy private.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Doesn't see that copy() bypasses the private constructor. Proposes suppressing the warnings.
  • Hire: Explains the public copy, moves the invariant into init, uses @ConsistentCopyVisibility.
  • Strong hire: Also plans the SDK binary-compat rollout (@ExposedCopyVisibility → major-version switch, binary validator), replaces copy with domain operations, and keeps the server as the trust boundary.

questions.contextHtml:
A food-delivery app (4M DAU, about 3.4M locally cached order rows across devices) stores order status in Room through a custom converter, and the user's theme in SharedPreferences:

enum class OrderStatus { PENDING, PREPARING, OUT_FOR_DELIVERY, DELIVERED, CANCELLED }

class Converters {
    @TypeConverter fun toInt(s: OrderStatus) = s.ordinal
    @TypeConverter fun toStatus(i: Int) = OrderStatus.entries[i]
}
prefs.edit().putInt("theme", theme.ordinal).apply()

In v8.4, a developer adds SCHEDULED after PENDING, "to keep the lifecycle in order", and adds SEPIA at the top of the Theme enum. At a 10% staged rollout, within 6 hours:

  • Support tickets: "my delivered order says out for delivery".
  • The theme flips for some users.
  • A new crash: ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: length=6; index=6 in toStatus, 0.4% of sessions.

The same week, the backend starts sending "status":"REFUNDED" and Moshi throws JsonDataException: Expected one of [PENDING, ...] but was REFUNDED. The team wants to just "halt the rollout and roll back".
questions.promptHtml: Walk me through mitigation, data repair under live traffic, and the long-term design.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Roll back to v8.3." But v8.4 has already written rows and prefs with the new ordinal meanings. Old code reading them misinterprets them, or crashes on index 5. A rollback doesn't un-write data.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Is the server the source of truth for order status? If it is, local rows are a cache and can be re-fetched.
    • Do rows have updatedAt or an app-version column, to tell which writer wrote them?
    • What's the reach: 10% of users times the period active?
    • Is the AIOOBE from rows written by 8.4 being read by 8.3, for example after a downgrade, or from the new REFUNDED mapping?
  2. Immediate mitigation:
    • Halt the staged rollout in Play Console. That's correct, but not sufficient.
    • Ship 8.4.1 fast. It restores the original constant order, with new constants appended. It also bumps the Room DB version with a migration that clears the cached orders table and forces a refetch, since the server is authoritative.
    • For prefs, write a themeSchema version key and reset the theme to default for anyone who ran 8.4. A wrong theme is cosmetic, and a reset is honest.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    • (a) The ordinal shift misinterprets stored ints. That explains the wrong statuses and themes.
    • (b) AIOOBE comes from ordinal 5 (CANCELLED under 8.4) or larger being read by a binary whose enum has fewer constants, or from a corrupted row.
    • (c) The Moshi exception is a separate issue, the unknown server value, with the same root theme: enums at a boundary aren't closed.
  4. How I'd verify each:
    • Query a debug device's DB (App Inspection → Database Inspector) before and after upgrade.
    • Crashlytics: split the AIOOBE by app version and "previous version" custom key.
    • Server logs: the first appearance of REFUNDED.
    • A unit test round-tripping every enum constant through the converter for both enum versions.
  5. Root cause:
    • ordinal is a declaration index, not an identity. Inserting a constant renumbers everything after it, so 3 meant DELIVERED in 8.3 and OUT_FOR_DELIVERY in 8.4.
    • Separately, deserializers treat enums as closed sets, but the server evolves independently, so unknown values throw (Moshi, kotlinx.serialization) or become null (Gson, which bypasses Kotlin null-safety; see chunk K1b).
  6. Fix: Short-term: 8.4.1 as above, plus an unknown fallback for network enums: 
    // Moshi: com.squareup.moshi.adapters.EnumJsonAdapter
Moshi.Builder()
    .add(OrderStatusDto::class.java,
         EnumJsonAdapter.create(OrderStatusDto::class.java).withUnknownFallback(OrderStatusDto.UNKNOWN))
    .build()

// kotlinx.serialization alternative: unknown enum values fall back to the property default
val json = Json { coerceInputValues = true }
@Serializable data class OrderDto(val status: OrderStatusDto = OrderStatusDto.UNKNOWN)
    Long-term: persist a stable, explicit code that's decoupled from both declaration order and constant names. 
    enum class OrderStatus(val code: String) {
    PENDING("pending"), SCHEDULED("scheduled"), PREPARING("preparing"),
    OUT_FOR_DELIVERY("ofd"), DELIVERED("delivered"), CANCELLED("cancelled"), UNKNOWN("unknown");
    companion object {
        private val byCode = entries.associateBy { it.code }
        fun fromCode(c: String?) = byCode[c] ?: UNKNOWN
    }
}
class Converters {
    @TypeConverter fun toCode(s: OrderStatus) = s.code
    @TypeConverter fun fromCode(c: String?) = OrderStatus.fromCode(c)
}
    • Add a Room migration that converts the INTEGER column to TEXT with a CASE mapping, using the 8.3 ordinal table, or simply clears the cache.
    • Room's built-in enum handling stores names (TEXT). That's better than ordinals, but a rename still breaks it, so I prefer an explicit code.
    • Map server DTO enums to domain enums at the boundary.
  7. Prevention:
    • A unit test pinning every persisted code: a "golden" list that fails if a code changes.
    • A lint/detekt rule banning .ordinal in converters and prefs.
    • A Room schema export checked into git so migrations get reviewed.
    • A contract test with the backend that includes unknown values.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why):
    • I wouldn't try to "repair" ambiguous rows heuristically. Rows written during the 8.4 window can't be disambiguated without a writer-version column, and the server copy is authoritative, so refetching is cheaper and correct.
    • I wouldn't persist name long-term without guarding renames.
    • I wouldn't make UNKNOWN silently render as a normal status. Show a neutral "updating..." state.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Does R8 obfuscation break name-based storage? → Generally no. The name string is passed to the enum constructor as a literal, so renaming the field doesn't change name(). Code that reflects on fields still needs keep rules. A custom code avoids the question entirely.
  • What about protobuf / Proto DataStore enums? → Proto stores numbers by design, but they're explicit field numbers you never reuse, so the same principle holds: stable explicit identifiers.
  • Users downgrade by sideloading the old APK? → The old code reads TEXT where it expects INTEGER. Room's version check will force a destructive fallback or crash. Decide fallbackToDestructiveMigrationOnDowngrade() explicitly.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A settings screen stored NotificationMode.ordinal. A designer-driven reorder of the enum, done to match the UI order, silently turned "Off" into "All" for a slice of users. The fix took a day. Rebuilding trust took a quarter.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "Roll back." Doesn't see that persisted data outlives the binary.
  • Hire: Identifies the ordinal shift, appends constants, migrates to a stable code, handles unknown server values.
  • Strong hire: Recognizes the 8.4-written data is ambiguous and uses server-authoritative refetch, plans prefs reset, considers the downgrade path, and adds golden tests and lint plus boundary DTO mapping.

questions.contextHtml:
Release 6.3.0 at 20% rollout. Crash-free users drop from 99.7% to 97.1% within 12 hours. Crashlytics top issues:

#1  java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class com.app.flags.FeatureFlags
        at com.app.home.HomeViewModel.<init>(HomeViewModel.kt:31)      48,210 events, 31k users
#2  java.lang.ExceptionInInitializerError
        at com.app.MainActivity.onCreate(MainActivity.kt:58)
    Caused by: kotlinx.serialization.json.internal.JsonDecodingException:
        Unexpected JSON token at offset 1873: Expected quotation mark '"' ...
        at com.app.flags.FeatureFlags.<clinit>(FeatureFlags.kt:14)        1,104 events, 1,090 users

The same release enabled R8 full mode, and someone points at #1 as an R8/class-stripping issue. ANR rate also rose from 0.31% to 0.52%, with main thread traces in FeatureFlags.<clinit> → SharedPreferencesImpl.awaitLoadedLocked. Affected users report the app "crashes every time I open it". The flags class:

object FeatureFlags {
    private val prefs = App.instance.getSharedPreferences("flags", Context.MODE_PRIVATE)
    private val config: FlagConfig =
        Json.decodeFromString(prefs.getString("cfg", null) ?: DEFAULT_JSON)
    val newCheckout get() = config.newCheckout
}
questions.promptHtml: What's going on, what do you do in the next hour, and what's the real fix?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "It's R8 removing the class, add a keep rule." That would ship a no-op fix, because #1 is a consequence of #2. Or: "Wrap the decode in try/catch" without understanding why users are stuck in a crash loop or why the ANR exists.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Do #1 and #2 occur for the same users and sessions? Check the Crashlytics user overlap or breadcrumbs: is #2 the first crash per process?
    • What wrote cfg? A remote-config fetch. Did the server or schema change, or can the write be truncated?
    • Does the kill switch run before FeatureFlags is touched? Probably not, if it lives inside the flags system.
  2. Immediate mitigation:
    • Halt the rollout.
    • Check whether the bad payload is server-side, for example a truncated response or a new field type. If it is, fix or roll back the server config right away. Users who already cached it still crash, though, because the crash happens at <clinit> before any refetch.
    • Ship 6.3.1, which treats a decode failure as "use defaults and delete cfg".
    • Tell support that clearing app data unblocks affected users in the meantime.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    • (a) A corrupted or incompatible cached JSON makes <clinit> throw. Then ExceptionInInitializerError occurs once per process and NoClassDefFoundError on every later access. That explains the 44:1 event ratio, and the crash on every launch because the bad value persists.
    • (b) R8 full mode stripping or renaming a serializer. If that were it, it would fail for all users with the same stack every time, not for ~1k users with a parse-offset error.
    • (c) The ANR is the same object doing disk IO and JSON parsing inside class init on the main thread at first access, independent of the crash.
  4. How I'd verify each:
    • Group Crashlytics by user and sort by time. The first event in each crashing session should be #2.
    • Pull a bad cfg from a beta tester device (adb shell run-as) or log its length and hash.
    • Reproduce with a unit test that decodes the stored payload.
    • Disable R8 full mode on a test build: #1 still reproduces with a bad payload, which rules R8 out.
    • Perfetto/ANR traces show <clinit> with the main thread waiting on the prefs load lock.
  5. Root cause:
    • JVM/ART class initialization runs <clinit> once. If it throws, the class is permanently marked erroneous for that process (see Q045). The first access gets ExceptionInInitializerError with the cause. Every later access, from the ViewModel, a worker or anything else, gets NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class, without the cause. That's why #1 dominates and looks unrelated.
    • The bad value is persisted, so every cold start fails the same way, which is a crash loop.
    • The ANR comes from the first access on main triggering a synchronous prefs read plus a JSON parse inside class init.
  6. Fix: Short-term (6.3.1): 
    object FeatureFlags {
    @Volatile private var config: FlagConfig? = null
    fun get(): FlagConfig = config ?: load().also { config = it }   // benign race: both threads compute same value
    private fun load(): FlagConfig {
        val prefs = App.instance.getSharedPreferences("flags", Context.MODE_PRIVATE)
        val raw = prefs.getString("cfg", null) ?: return FlagConfig.DEFAULT
        return try {
            Json { ignoreUnknownKeys = true }.decodeFromString<FlagConfig>(raw)
        } catch (e: kotlinx.serialization.SerializationException) {
            prefs.edit().remove("cfg").apply()          // break the crash loop
            FlagConfig.DEFAULT
        } catch (e: IllegalArgumentException) {
            prefs.edit().remove("cfg").apply()
            FlagConfig.DEFAULT
        }
    }
}
    Long-term:
    • Make flags an injected @Singleton class (Hilt) whose loading happens off the main thread, warmed in Application.onCreate on a background dispatcher and exposed as StateFlow<FlagConfig> with defaults.
    • Validate payloads at fetch time before persisting them: write to a temp key, decode, then swap.
    • Version the schema.
  7. Prevention:
    • Rule: <clinit> (object/companion property initializers) must be trivial, with no IO, parsing or anything that can throw.
    • Crash-loop detection: increment a launch counter in Application.onCreate and clear it after 10 s of healthy run. If it reaches 3, start in a safe mode that wipes caches and skips optional init.
    • Alert on NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class as a signal to look for the matching ExceptionInInitializerError.
    • Fuzz and old-payload tests for config decoding.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why):
    • I wouldn't add R8 keep rules "just in case". That adds noise and binary size, and delays the real fix.
    • I wouldn't catch Throwable in <clinit> and keep going silently. Catch the specific decode exceptions, log a non-fatal and fall back.
    • I wouldn't move parsing into by lazy alone. lazy rethrows on every access and retries, which is better than an erroneous class, but it still leaves the crash loop and the main-thread cost.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does NoClassDefFoundError have no "Caused by"? → ART throws it on later accesses to an erroneous class. Some runtimes attach the original as the cause, but you can't rely on it. Always look for the first ExceptionInInitializerError in the process.
  • Could the same happen with an enum or companion? → Yes. Any static initializer: companion property initializers live in the outer class's <clinit> (Q046).
  • How would you push the fix to users who crash before any network call? → Only an app update, or the safe-mode logic, can help. That's why crash-loop detection must not depend on remote config.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A localization object parsed a downloaded strings bundle in its initializer. One truncated download bricked the app for 0.8% of users until they cleared data. The dashboard showed NoClassDefFoundError from 30 different call sites, which looked like 30 bugs and was actually one.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Chases R8 or multidex. Can't connect #1 and #2.
  • Hire: Explains the erroneous-class mechanism, fixes the decode with a fallback, deletes the bad value.
  • Strong hire: Also explains the crash loop and why server-side fixes don't reach cached users, ties the ANR to <clinit> IO on main, adds crash-loop safe mode, validate-before-persist and the "trivial clinit" rule.

questions.contextHtml:
A shopping app's product grid has a filter memo cache:

data class FilterQuery(
    val category: String,
    val brandIds: Set<Long>,
    val priceRange: IntRange,
    val hiddenIds: Set<Long>       // products the user hid; power users have 15k–20k
)
private val memo = HashMap<FilterQuery, List<Product>>()

fun visibleProducts(q: FilterQuery): List<Product> =
    memo.getOrPut(q) { compute(q) }  // called from onBindViewHolder for "badge" logic, ~6x per frame while scrolling

On a Galaxy A-series device, scroll jank is 22% janky frames for users with large hiddenIds, versus 3% for others. A Perfetto trace on RenderThread/main shows FilterQuery.hashCode → AbstractSet.hashCode taking about 1.8 ms per call, and the occasional FilterQuery.equals → AbstractSet.equals → containsAll taking about 2.5 ms. GC is noticeable too, but the team's first idea is "switch to Sequences" or "it's GC, increase the heap".
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix. Quantify the problem.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use Sequence" or "use ConcurrentHashMap". Neither changes the work done per lookup. "Make the cache an LRU" also ignores the per-lookup cost.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Does FilterQuery change during a scroll? It doesn't: the user isn't touching filters, so the answer is constant across frames.
    • How often is it constructed? A new instance per bind, which matters for equals.
    • Are hiddenIds sets shared instances, or rebuilt from the DB on each emission?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Compute visibleProducts once per query change in the ViewModel and pass the result to the adapter. Binding then does no cache lookups at all.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    • (a) Generated hashCode isn't cached and recurses into Set.hashCode, which iterates all elements. That's O(n) per lookup.
    • (b) On a hash hit with a different instance, generated equals calls Set.equals, which does containsAll: another O(n) with hash probes per element.
    • (c) GC from boxed Long iteration is a secondary effect. Iterating a HashSet<Long> allocates only the iterator, so GC is mostly from other bind work.
  4. How I'd verify each:
    • Perfetto with custom trace sections (androidx.tracing.trace("memoLookup") { }).
    • A microbenchmark (Jetpack Microbenchmark) of hashCode() with 20k ids.
    • The allocation tracker in the Android Studio profiler to check the GC hypothesis.
  5. Root cause: The math: 6 lookups per frame × (1.8 ms hash + ~2.5 ms equals on a hit with a fresh instance) ≈ 25 ms per frame in the worst case, against a 16.7 ms budget at 60 Hz. With hash alone, 6 × 1.8 ≈ 10.8 ms, which leaves only about 6 ms for everything else. Hence the jank, only for users with large sets.
    • Data class hashCode is recomputed on every call, unlike String.hashCode, which is cached. It combines each property's hashCode().
    • Set<Long>.hashCode() sums element hashes over 20k boxed Longs, with pointer chasing on each, so it's cache-unfriendly on little cores.
    • Generated equals short-circuits only on this === other. Two different FilterQuery instances wrapping the same Set instance still reach Set.equals. That in turn short-circuits on identity (AbstractSet.equals checks o == this first), but only if the set instances are shared, and here they're rebuilt per emission.
  6. Fix: Short-term: remove the per-bind lookup (step 2). It's a design bug, not a hashing bug. Long-term: if a value key over large collections is still needed, make it cheap. 
    class FilterQuery(
    val category: String,
    val brandIds: Set<Long>,
    val priceRange: IntRange,
    val hiddenIds: Set<Long>,
    private val hiddenVersion: Long          // bumped by the repository when hiddenIds changes
) {
    // Precomputed once; safe only because every field is immutable
    private val hash = arrayOf(category, brandIds, priceRange, hiddenVersion).contentHashCode()
    override fun hashCode() = hash
    override fun equals(other: Any?): Boolean =
        this === other || (other is FilterQuery && hash == other.hash &&
            category == other.category && priceRange == other.priceRange &&
            hiddenVersion == other.hiddenVersion && brandIds == other.brandIds)
}
    • The key uses a version/fingerprint for the big set instead of its contents, so cost becomes O(brands), which is small.
    • It's no longer a data class, because I'm customizing both methods and don't want copy() to bypass the version contract. An alternative is to keep the data class and override hashCode/equals in its body, which the compiler allows.
    • Use LongArray or a primitive set where storage matters, avoiding about 16 bytes of boxing per element.
  7. Prevention:
    • Add a Macrobenchmark FrameTimingMetric for the grid scroll with a 20k-hidden-ids fixture.
    • Review rule: no data classes holding large collections used as map keys, remember/key inputs or diff payloads without a cheap identity.
    • Trace sections in hot paths.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why):
    • The version-based key trusts the repository to bump versions. A missed bump means stale results, so I'd centralize it in the single writer.
    • I wouldn't cache hashCode in a class with mutable fields.
    • "Sequences" changes nothing here, and enlarging the heap hides symptoms.
    • Lazily caching the hash (by lazy) adds a lock and an object per instance. A precomputed val is cheaper when instances are created rarely.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why is String.hashCode fine as a key but this isn't? → String caches its hash in a field after the first computation. Data class hashes aren't cached.
  • Does Compose have the same issue? → Yes, if a large data class is used as a remember(key) or LazyColumn key, its equals/hashCode run during composition. Stability is covered in chunk K7.
  • What if two different queries collide on hash? → equals still compares fields, so the result stays correct, just slower on a collision.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "selected filters" data class holding a 10k-element set was the key of a distinct in a reactive pipeline. CPU on the filter screen dropped by 70% after it switched to a version-stamped key. Nobody had suspected hashCode, because "it's generated".

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Proposes Sequences or GC tuning. Doesn't know generated hashCode walks nested collections.
  • Hire: Identifies the O(n) hashCode/equals, does the frame-budget math, removes the per-bind lookup.
  • Strong hire: Also explains the identity short-circuits and why rebuilt sets defeat them, designs a version-stamped key with a precomputed hash, and adds macrobenchmarks and review rules.

questions.contextHtml:
A tech lead asks for a cart that's "the same everywhere, just make it a singleton". The app has 25 feature modules and about 1,400 JVM unit tests. A developer ships:

object CartStore {
    private val items = mutableMapOf<String, Int>()
    lateinit var api: CartApi                 // set in Application.onCreate
    fun add(sku: String) { items[sku] = (items[sku] ?: 0) + 1 }
    fun count() = items.values.sum()
}

Within two weeks:

  • CI flakiness rises from 1% to 7% of runs: tests pass alone and fail in the full suite.
  • A QA bug: after logout and login as another user, the previous user's cart shows.
  • A crash: UninitializedPropertyAccessException: lateinit property api has not been initialized, 0.05% of sessions, from a BroadcastReceiver cold start.
questions.promptHtml: What's ambiguous in the requirement, and how would you design this?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add CartStore.clear() in @Before and in logout." That patches the symptoms of global mutable state. It doesn't address the init-order crash or testability.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • What does "the same everywhere" mean? Within a process? Across devices, which would need a server cart? Across process death, which needs persistence?
    • Per user or per install?
    • Must the cart survive app kill? Each answer changes the scope: process-level vs user session vs persistent.
  2. Immediate mitigation:
    • Call CartStore.clear() on logout as a hotfix for the leak between users.
    • Mark the flaky tests and quarantine them while the refactor lands.
    • Fix the receiver crash by making sure the receiver path doesn't touch CartStore, or initialize api lazily from the Application.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    • (a) Shared global state across tests in the same JVM. Gradle reuses test JVMs (forkEvery defaults to 0), so object state leaks between test classes, and the failures depend on execution order.
    • (b) Process-lifetime scope doesn't match user-session lifetime, which explains the cross-user cart.
    • (c) An init-order dependency: the lateinit is set in Application.onCreate, but some entry points, or ContentProviders initialized before Application.onCreate, or tests, touch it first or skip it.
  4. How I'd verify each:
    • Run the suite with forkEvery = 1. The flakiness disappears, which confirms state leakage.
    • Reproduce logout → login.
    • Check the stack of the crash: receiver → CartStore.add before api is set, for example in test or instrumentation setups or alternate init paths.
  5. Root cause: A Kotlin object gives you a process-wide instance with no lifecycle, no constructor injection and no reset. The requirement "single instance" was implemented as "global static state". The real requirements are one instance per user session and a swappable implementation for tests.
  6. Fix: 
    interface CartRepository { val count: StateFlow<Int>; suspend fun add(sku: String); suspend fun clear() }

@Singleton
class DefaultCartRepository @Inject constructor(
    private val api: CartApi,                 // constructor-injected: no lateinit, no init order
    private val dao: CartDao                  // persisted if the cart must survive process death
) : CartRepository { /* ... */ }

@Module @InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
interface CartModule { @Binds fun bind(impl: DefaultCartRepository): CartRepository }
    • "Singleton" now means one per DI component. If the cart is per user, scope it to a user-session component, or clear it in a logout hook owned by the session manager.
    • Tests construct DefaultCartRepository(fakeApi, fakeDao) directly, giving fresh state per test with no global.
    • Keep object for stateless things: pure functions, constants, data object states.
  7. Prevention:
    • A detekt/lint rule or review guideline: no mutable state or lateinit in objects in feature code.
    • A test that logs in as A, adds items, logs out, logs in as B and asserts the cart is empty.
    • Keep test JVM reuse, since it's faster, but treat order-dependence as a bug.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why):
    • object is zero-setup and fine for leaf utilities. DI adds wiring and some build time.
    • I wouldn't use forkEvery = 1 as the fix. It multiplies CI time, from ~4 min to ~20+ min for 1,400 tests, and hides the design issue.
    • I wouldn't add a reset() "for tests only" to a production object. It leaks test concerns into prod.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Is object thread-safe for this map? → The initialization is thread-safe (Q045). Mutations to mutableMapOf aren't. That's a separate concurrency bug once coroutines on Dispatchers.Default call add. See chunk C8.
  • Can Hilt inject into a Kotlin object? → Not through constructor injection, because an object has no injectable constructor. You'd need EntryPoints, which is a smell for this use.
  • What if the app has no DI framework? → Manual DI: create one instance in Application (an app container) and pass it down. That's still not global mutable state.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "session" object kept the previous account's auth token after account switching. The bug surfaced as one user seeing another's order history on shared family tablets. The postmortem rule became: per-user state never lives in a process-scoped static.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Adds clear() calls everywhere and moves on.
  • Hire: Explains global state leaking across tests and users, moves to a DI-scoped singleton with constructor injection.
  • Strong hire: Decodes the ambiguous requirement into lifetimes (process, user session, persistent), ties the crash to init order and lateinit, sets team guidance for when object is appropriate, and gives a CI cost argument against forkEvery.

questions.contextHtml:
You're running the post-incident review for a 0.08% session crash that lasted three releases on a 6M-MAU news app:

kotlin.NoWhenBranchMatchedException
    at com.app.article.ArticleFragment.render(ArticleFragment.kt:88)

It reproduces only after process death ("Don't keep activities" plus backgrounding, or low-RAM devices like 2 GB Android Go). The ViewModel stores the current state in SavedStateHandle:

sealed class ArticleState : java.io.Serializable {
    object Loading : ArticleState()
    object Offline : ArticleState()
    data class Loaded(val id: String, val title: String) : ArticleState()
}
// ViewModel
savedStateHandle["state"] = state            // Serializable into Bundle
val state = savedStateHandle.get<ArticleState>("state") ?: ArticleState.Loading

// Fragment
fun render(s: ArticleState) = when (s) {
    ArticleState.Loading -> showSpinner()
    ArticleState.Offline -> showOffline()
    is ArticleState.Loaded -> showArticle(s)
}

Earlier "fixes" in the timeline: someone added else -> showSpinner(), which stopped the crash, but then users reported "infinite spinner after returning to the app". That was reverted. Red herring in the timeline: a Fragment library upgrade in the same period.
questions.promptHtml: Write the root cause and corrective actions for the review. Why did the else "fix" produce an infinite spinner?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Process death loses state; just reload." Or "The when is missing a branch, add else." Neither explains why a declared branch failed to match an object of the right type.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Which states are restored when it crashes? Breadcrumbs show Loading or Offline, never Loaded.
    • Is Java serialization the only persistence path? Yes, SavedStateHandle → Bundle.putSerializable.
    • Did the Fragment upgrade change restore timing? It's checkable, but it doesn't explain a type that matches yet fails to match.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Change the object checks to is checks (is ArticleState.Loading ->). That's a type test, which any deserialized instance passes. It's a one-line, low-risk hotfix while the root fix lands.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    • (a) Java deserialization creates a second instance of each object, because no readResolve is generated. when with a constant branch compares by equals, and a plain object's equals is identity, so nothing matches and the exhaustive when's hidden default throws NoWhenBranchMatchedException.
    • (b) A Fragment upgrade side effect. It doesn't fit the per-type pattern.
    • (c) A ProGuard/R8 renaming of serialized classes. That would throw InvalidClassException/ClassNotFoundException, not a when miss.
  4. How I'd verify each:
    • A JVM unit test serializing ArticleState.Loading through ObjectOutputStream/ObjectInputStream. Then restored == ArticleState.Loading is false and restored === ArticleState.Loading is false.
    • Decompile render (Kotlin Bytecode → Decompile) to confirm the constant branches are equality checks on the compiler version in use.
    • Reproduce on device with "Don't keep activities".
  5. Root cause:
    • A Kotlin object is a singleton by convention: INSTANCE in <clinit>. Java serialization doesn't run constructors or <clinit> for the restored value. It allocates a fresh instance unless the class defines readResolve(), and the Kotlin compiler doesn't add that for objects, which is why the IDE inspection exists.
    • when (s) { ArticleState.Loading -> } is an equality test. With a plain object, equality is identity, so the restored Loading matches no branch.
    • The else "fix" made it worse in a quieter way. It mapped every restored instance, including Offline, to the spinner. Any code elsewhere checking state == ArticleState.Loading to decide whether to start loading was also false, so the reload never triggered. That's the infinite spinner.
  6. Fix: Short-term: is checks plus data object (equality by type, Kotlin 1.9+): 
    sealed class ArticleState : java.io.Serializable {
    data object Loading : ArticleState() { private fun readResolve(): Any = Loading }
    data object Offline : ArticleState() { private fun readResolve(): Any = Offline }
    data class Loaded(val id: String, val title: String) : ArticleState()
}
    data object fixes ==, and readResolve restores identity for any === or identity-based code. Long-term: don't persist derived UI state at all. Save the inputs, articleId (a String), in SavedStateHandle, and re-derive state on restore: start in Loading and reload from cache or network. That makes process death a normal code path. Use @Parcelize or primitives instead of java.io.Serializable where something must be saved, since it's faster and explicit.
  7. Prevention:
    • Enable the "Serializable object must implement readResolve" inspection as an error.
    • Add a test utility that round-trips every saved-state type through Bundle/Parcel (or Java serialization) and asserts equality.
    • Run process-death testing in QA: "Don't keep activities", adb shell am kill <pkg> while backgrounded.
    • Review rule: object states in sealed hierarchies must be data object.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do (and why):
    • An else branch on sealed types hides future cases and, as shown, masks identity bugs. Avoid it.
    • I wouldn't switch serialization to Gson "because it's easier". Reflective deserializers can also allocate a second instance of an object.
    • kotlinx.serialization handles objects by returning the existing instance, so it's acceptable if a serialized form is needed.
    • Saving the whole Loaded article in the Bundle risks TransactionTooLargeException (the Binder transaction buffer is about 1 MB, shared per process), which is another reason to save only IDs.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Would is ArticleState.Loading alone have prevented the crash? → Yes, for the when. But any == or === comparisons elsewhere still break, so the type-level fix (data object plus readResolve) is the real one.
  • Do enums have this problem? → No. Java serialization handles enums specially by name and returns the canonical constant.
  • Why didn't unit tests catch it? → Tests never crossed a serialization boundary. The ViewModel and Fragment shared the in-memory instance.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A checkout flow's object Idle state came back from saved state as a second instance. The "Pay" button stayed disabled after process death, because its enablement checked state == Idle. Conversion dipped on low-RAM devices for weeks before anyone correlated it with process death.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Treats it as "process death loses state" and adds else.
  • Hire: Explains that Java deserialization creates a new object instance and that the when constant branch uses equality. Fixes it with data object or is checks.
  • Strong hire: Explains why the else produced the infinite spinner, adds readResolve for identity, redesigns to save inputs rather than derived state, and adds round-trip tests, process-death QA and the inspection as an error.
